utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Good morning, everyone. Please continue, Mr. Nicholls.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honours. Thank you. Just before we continue. A little bit of clean-up from yesterday. I'd move to tender 65 ter 04397 and 04398. Those are the two documents I used in cross yesterday. I apologise for not tendering them at the time. They weren't they on my list so I forgot.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Any objections?

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBINSON
utterances.text: No, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: We'll admit them both.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Now shall we give the numbers.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: 65 ter number 04397 receives Exhibit Number D3996 --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: I'm sorry, we should assign P numbers.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: P numbers, excuse me. 65 ter number 04397 is P6496, Your Honours. 65 ter number 04398 is Exhibit Number P6497, Your Honours. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Thank you. Could I have P00195, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: And what I'm going to do now, just briefly before we get back started, is touch on the issue of the Bratunac Brigade soldier wounded at Kravica which we talked about a bit yesterday.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: These documents weren't on my list, but I sent them to Mr. Robinson this morning. So P00195, please. Okay, there we see it. This is a log of wounded soldiers. If we go to page 2, please, of both. We'll see when the English comes up, on the first line, yeah, 13 July 1995 at 1730 hours, date and time of wounding, Miroslav Stanojevic, Red Beret, wounded at Kravica. If we look at the one just below him, we see Rade Cuturic, wounded at Kravica ten minutes later, and this is the special police person whose hands were burned that we've spoken about a lot. So same time, same place. And now if we could have 65 ter --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Was this exhibit admitted through a 92 bis witness as an associated exhibit?

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: I believe so, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Now if I could have 65 ter 25596. And just very quickly, this is again a registration sheet for the same soldier in the Bratunac Brigade, Miroslav Stanojevic. And if we go to page 3 of the English, page 2 of the Serbian, we just see report of wounding of this man at Kravica on 13 July.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: If you look at number 14, Mr. Popovic, you see wound of the right elbow, serious wound, wounded while taking captured Muslims into custody. So you agree with me, Mr. Popovic, that this shows there was a Bratunac Brigade member wounded at Kravica on the 13th?

utterances.speaker: VUJADIN POPOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, yes. Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: May I tender that, please?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, this will be admitted as Exhibit P6498.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Mr. Popovic, what's that big book you brought with you today?

utterances.speaker: VUJADIN POPOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mr. Nicholls, I brought Milan Vujaklija's book, he was a lexicographer in the former Yugoslavia. He was the best, and it is a lexicon of foreign phrases, and if you don't mind, I'd like to read out what the entry for "balija" says. This edition is 1991. Will you allow me to read that out?

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: No, sorry. You can do that on re-direct if Mr. Karadzic would like you to. Now we're still on the 13th of July back at the Hotel Fontana that night where you stay, according to your statement, and Mr. Beara is also in Bratunac that night with you, correct, 13 July?

utterances.speaker: VUJADIN POPOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. That was the first time on that day that I saw him during my stay in Bratunac.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: VUJADIN POPOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Before that we did not have any contact.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreter's note: Could the witness please come closer to the microphone when speaking. We can barely hear him. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Now, as Drina Corps security chief you would have known and you would have had to know that the town of Bratunac was -- the town centre was literally flooded with thousands of prisoners that night; correct?

utterances.speaker: VUJADIN POPOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: As far as I know, in the centre there weren't these thousands. I parked the car in front of Fontana. There's a big parking-lot there and then I entered Fontana. Well, I did not notice when I passed by then -- well, maybe but then it wasn't in the centre, not there.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Okay. The Trial Chamber's been to Bratunac so I'm not going to bring up an aerial. You knew that Muslims were being held in the Vuk Karadzic school, a hangar behind the school, in the stadium, and in buses parked outside Vihor garages, and in front of the municipality building, and all around the centre, right, when you were in the Hotel Fontana that night; right?

utterances.speaker: VUJADIN POPOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mr. Nicholls, when I passed by, the prisoners stayed behind at Sandici, Livade. As far as I know, in Bratunac, there were only the people who had been separated from Potocari and they probably arrived just after me.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Okay. Let's be very clear. When you spent the night of 13 July in Bratunac, you were not aware that thousands of men who had been captured along the Bratunac-Konjevic Polje road had been brought to Bratunac and kept in those places I just read out, Vuk Karadzic school, et cetera, you didn't know that that night?

utterances.speaker: VUJADIN POPOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I knew that they were taken prisoner and that they were transported there, but I did not see them. At night I was at the motel --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreter's note: We can no longer hear the witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Mr. Popovic, if you could speak to the microphone.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I'm saying that I knew they were there but I did not see them. At 9.00, I mean, after that I didn't leave the motel. I went to sleep.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Okay. Now let's be clear. You knew they were there. Are you now saying you admit that you know that all the men captured along the road were there, not just what you said a minute ago, the men separated in Potocari?

utterances.speaker: VUJADIN POPOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In my statement I put it very clearly. I don't know actually if it entered my statement. I know full well, I remember as I was passing through Kasaba that Malinic was already stopping some buses and there were about ten buses there, parked, and that's why I couldn't park right next to him. I had to park further down --

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Sorry --

utterances.speaker: VUJADIN POPOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: -- that is to say that it was already being prepared, the evacuation, from there.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Okay. Answer my question, please. On the night of the 13th, did you know that in addition to the men separated in Potocari and brought to Bratunac, that thousands of men who had been captured along the Bratunac-Konjevic Polje road were also brought to Bratunac?

utterances.speaker: VUJADIN POPOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I tell you that I knew, but I did not see them. This is the third time I'm saying that: I did not see them.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: All right. Okay. So you knew that men from the road were brought to Bratunac, not just those separated, which is what you said a few minutes ago, that you thought it was just the men separated in Potocari?

utterances.speaker: VUJADIN POPOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: VUJADIN POPOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, no. I'm saying, when I arrived, I knew that they had come too. But after talking to Beara and all the rest, the column probably went in front of him. I'm not sure now. I cannot calculate now, but the column arrived but I did not see them --

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: I'm not --

utterances.speaker: VUJADIN POPOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: -- it's not that I saw them.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Okay. I'm not asking what you saw. All right. Not at the moment. Try to answer this with a yes or no if you can. Did you know that thousands of Muslim prisoners, thousands plural, were held in Bratunac on the night of the 13th? While you were there I'm speaking about.

utterances.speaker: VUJADIN POPOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm saying for the third time that I did know.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Okay. Let's talk about how those men were treated, and I'll just briefly go over the trial judgement in your case. Paragraph 400 talks about the extremely cramped conditions in the Vuk Karadzic school and the hangar behind the school. Paragraph 401 talks about how at the Vuk Karadzic school, the prisoners were forced to leave their bags and food outside the building and were not interviewed or asked to give their names. Paragraph 402 said that the prisoners asked for food and water. They were given some water but no food, and when they complained, the guards fired over their heads and threatened them. Paragraph 403 says that in the vehicles parked at various locations through Bratunac town, the prisoners were provided with little or no food and when water was provided it was not sufficient. Paragraph 404 states that some prisoners detained in various locations in Bratunac town were beaten by members of Bosnian Serb forces. Screams, moans, and bursts of fire were heard in the vicinity of the places of detention. In the Vuk Karadzic school, prisoners were beaten on way to the toilet and therefore chose to relieve themselves where they were. And there's testimony in this case at P00769, e-court page 69, about people being taken out of the buses and trucks behind the Vihor garage and this witness heard screams, people yelling: "Stop that, stop that," and bursts of fire. So men beaten, men taken out, and screams heard, IDs taken, inadequate, if any, food and water. Is this standard procedure for the way the VRS treats its prisoners? I'm asking you as Drina Corps security chief. Is that standard procedure to beat, kill, starve, and deny water to prisoners?

utterances.speaker: VUJADIN POPOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That was not standard procedure.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Okay. If that's not standard procedure, since you're in the centre of town, five-minutes' walk from all of these places of detention where all of these terrible things were happening, as a trained security chief and operative, didn't that tip you off that something might not be quite right since the prisoners are being beaten and killed all around you?

utterances.speaker: VUJADIN POPOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mr. Nicholls, I repeat, I did not see them. How could I know then at that moment when that was happening? I did not know then that it was happening at all.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Okay. Thank you. You've answered. You didn't know. Let's go to the 14th of July. I want to move through this quite quickly. Please put your statement down and don't read it. Thank you. I'm not going to go through your statement again. You describe what your alleged movements are in the morning and where you go, but you were in Bratunac in the morning. Very early you go to Zvornik Brigade. You come back to Bratunac. And according to you, around noon that day, you, with the convoy of prisoners, set off from Bratunac to Zvornik; correct?

utterances.speaker: VUJADIN POPOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Now, that means you drive past the Kravica warehouse again; right?

utterances.speaker: VUJADIN POPOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Mr. Karadzic's witness here, Aleksandar Tesic, at T 35324 to 35326, says he left Bratunac at about 11.00 that day. He's not exactly sure, between 10.00 and noon, and he sees 200 to 300 bodies stacked up a metre and a half high in front of the Kravica warehouse. Did you happen to notice that when you were passing by the Kravica warehouse for the third time in these two days?

utterances.speaker: VUJADIN POPOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, you see, I remember that day as we were passing that the corpses were covered with hay. Now, was it at that moment or when we were returning from Zvornik, I cannot say for sure. But the corpses were covered with hay. Perhaps this left some impression on him that this was a heap and all the rest, but it was hay. I think this was done on the evening of the 13th -- no, not on the 13th in the evening, but the 13th immediately afterwards or on the 14th because of the transportation on the road. And I remember for sure that the corpses were covered with hay. So please -- anyway I'm telling you all of this to the best of my recollection.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Okay. And you also know that your superior, Colonel Beara, on the night of the 13th ordered that the bodies from the Kravica warehouse be buried in Glogova.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: That's at P00345, e-court pages 12 to 13, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: You know that, night of the 13th, while you were asleep, I guess, according to you, Beara ordered somebody to take all those bodies out of the warehouse and bury them in a pit in Glogova?

utterances.speaker: VUJADIN POPOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mr. Nicholls, how can I know that at that point in time, that he ordered that and -- I mean, I did not know then.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Okay. So -- just so I try to understand, I think what you're trying say is that -- well, you don't dispute that he ordered that, do you? That was proven in your own trial. Are you disputing that he ordered the bodies to be buried?

utterances.speaker: VUJADIN POPOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I cannot confirm it or deny it because then I did not know about that.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Okay. So -- so you and Beara are in Bratunac. You and Beara are staying at the Hotel Fontana on the night of the 13th. Beara is ordering all the bodies buried who had been murdered at Kravica warehouse that day. You are his direct subordinate in the professional line and you're isolated in some kind of bubble where you don't know what's going on. That's the story; right?

utterances.speaker: VUJADIN POPOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Not my story, Mr. Nicholls. If you read the statement and if you look at the sequence of events that followed and the statements of other people, that's it. I went to sleep. I had barely slept the previous night. Now, he was there with Pecanac, and where he went after that and who he saw and what he did, I don't know. As a matter of fact, it was only here at the trial itself that I found out that he was asking for some machine and these talks, and I simply don't know. I was asleep at the time.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Just so you know, you keep referring to it's in your statement. I've read it. I don't accept what's in your statement. I'm just giving you our position. We don't accept that you were truthful in your statement. All right. Now, let's go further on on the 14th -- sorry, one more question on that. The other evidence in this case is that the civilian protection knew the bodies were being buried, that Miroslav Deronjic and the authorities in Bratunac knew that the bodies were being buried in Glogova. You drive right past the Glogova mass burial site on the 14th, which is the day they're being buried there, and you're still saying you didn't know about it; right?

utterances.speaker: VUJADIN POPOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: We have to clarify the bit before that and then we're going to deal with this. First of all, you know during the investigation who talked to Beara when and you know that I did not attend these conversations. You can say that you're not taking my statement into account, but you know that I was not present during these conversations. Secondly, on the morning of the 14th, there weren't -- there wasn't any digging going on at that time. I did not notice this on the other side of the road, about 100 metres away, 200 metres away, I really wasn't paying attention. I was leading the convoy. Well, in the morning it wasn't, maybe it was in the afternoon, but I did not notice. So why say that?

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Okay. 14th of July, Orahovac, that's what I'm going to talk to you now about, the 14th of July, Orahovac, the school. In your trial, you contested evidence that placed you at the school in Orahovac, and that's laid out in your final brief in that trial at paragraphs 493 to 495, where you challenged the testimony of a military policeman who said you were there. And that didn't work. In the judgement at paragraphs 1108 to 1112, the Trial Chamber, the honourable Trial Chamber, found that you were present at Orahovac. And so what you've done in this statement now, now that your Defence said, "I wasn't there at all," didn't work, is come up with a story to fit your presence at the Orahovac school, once again as an innocent bystander; right?

utterances.speaker: VUJADIN POPOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't remember that at all, that we claimed, yes, no. I said to the best of my recollection what the time was when I was there and for how long I was there. That can be confirmed.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Okay. Now I want to talk about how you describe the conditions and the way the prisoners were treated at the school, and you can look at it if you want. This is paragraph 50 of your statement. "I arrived in front of the school in Orahovac at about 1.00 in the afternoon. There were many people dressed in civilian clothes and military uniforms there. The prisoners of war had already been put in the school sports hall. I looked into the hall from the door and saw that some prisoners were sitting on the floor, while others were standing or moving about. There were between 400 and 500 prisoners in the hall. In front of the school, there were between six and eight buses and some people were still on them because the security guards thought they would lose control of the prisoners if they too were put in the sports hall. These buses were sent to some other place." That's what you say in your statement. Some prisoners are sitting on the floor, others are walking around, and that the remaining prisoners were sent somewhere else. Now, I'm putting it to you, you are not telling the truth. That you are saying there was plenty of room and people were walking around and comfortable and then the remaining prisoners were taken somewhere else in order to hide the terrible, terrible conditions those prisoners were kept in in that gym before they were executed?

utterances.speaker: VUJADIN POPOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mr. Nicholls, that is absolutely not correct. I have no reason to hide that because that's really the way it was. That's really the way it was. You were there and you saw it, that 2 and a half thousand people fit in that room, that is simply impossible. And I brought 30 buses. Nobody was standing there. And one longer bus. Quite simply, it's not correct. This hall was not crowded. Some were sitting there, some were standing, some were walking. A school desk was in there too. It was a bit in front of the door, and water was distributed through that desk. They would take water, empty the other vessels, and so on. Simply, that is not correct. There is always exaggeration on the other side too, you have to understand that.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Okay. That's really the way it was. That's what you said. Let's hear what the people who were kept in the hall said about the way it really was.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: KDZ039, Your Honours, protected witness. His statement is P03940, I'm talking about e-court pages 34 to 35 now.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: "While there were just a few of us, the ones who arrived with the four buses" - and, I'm sorry, I'll say this man arrived on the night of the 13th - "the conditions were all right. But when the warehouse got full and when the last trucks and buses had been -- brought people in and when no more could enter the gym, then we were told to stand up, to face the door, and to step backwards, and then we were stepping backwards. And they were firing over our heads and saying: Back, back, back, we will shoot you. And that's what we kept doing until we made rooms for even the last ones to enter. And then when they entered, we were told to sit down. And then when we sat down, those who managed to sit down first were able to sit down. The others could only sit in our lap. There was no more floor space for others to sit and that's when it got very stuffy, tight, and we wanted to suffocate." I'll read you one more. KDZ064, who was there on the 14th, convoy you brought. "How full was the sports hall when you entered it? "When I entered, over half of it was full. And when everybody entered, there was very little space left, but we all sat down crunched and squeezed. We were sitting so tight that we could not move from the place that we were assigned. Nobody offered us any food. Some prisoners were asked to bring water but there were just too many of us. If they started from one end, they could only give water to two lines of people, so we were always thirsty. If you didn't experience that, then you can never know that water was the most beautiful thing in the world. Nobody wanted bread, but if somebody had brought you water, I believe that we would have drank 2 litres at once. That's how important water is. And that's why I'm saying today that water is even more important than bread. We were thirsty, and if you have never been thirsty, you don't know the feeling. You cannot imagine the feeling."

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: That's at P00769, Your Honours. E-court page 98.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: That man couldn't walk up to a table and get a glass of water. Are you saying these men in that school you took them to are not telling the truth?

utterances.speaker: VUJADIN POPOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I have no comment to make on this. Maybe there are truthful things in that, but I'm telling you the hall was not so overcrowded. We gave them water. They took it over the heads of other people and returned the jugs. I believe there were five to six or eight guards there, and it was a problem for them to guard all these people. And everybody who gets out exaggerates their story a little. I mean, everybody exaggerates, why not? I'm really sorry that any of this happened, but some of these things really don't hold water. They're not true.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: All right. So you're saying those statements -- all right. All right. Rocevic school where you also admit to being on the 14th. We're not to your 15th alibi yet, 14th, Rocevic school. You basically try to paint the same picture. This is your statement, paragraph 52. "... I saw about 200 or 300 prisoners. I noticed canisters with water at the front door. Some locals had brought some bread." Testimony in this case from Srecko Acimovic, P00343, e-court page 10, he's talking about being at the school on the 14th. "I heard shouts from the gym. People were screaming for water. They wanted to go to the bathroom. The temperatures were running very high around that time."

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: And if I could go to private session for one moment, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: We are in open session, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Now we may need to be careful. We're in open session. I don't know what Mr. Karadzic is going to say to clarify.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Mr. Nicholls, the purpose of going into private session was to tell the name of the witness in question?

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Also that --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: The situation that may identify the witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, I now see the point.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Karadzic.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: And, sorry, Your Honours, that testimony -- that -- what I read out was in private session in the previous case, I believe, that's why as well.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: The transcript was admitted?

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Pursuant to Rule 92 bis?

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Karadzic.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] In the interpretation -- I mean, the interpreters did not catch what five to a square metre was. We did not get in interpretation -- I mean the witness did not get in interpretation what it means.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Five persons per square metre. I think I can say that in public session, prisoners inside the gym.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Now, you are again not telling the truth about the conditions in those schools because the way those prisoners were kept in those schools when you were there indicated that they were not being sent for exchange, that they were not being treated the way prisoners who were going to exchange are going to be treated, that they were treated as people who were going to be killed, which is why you're minimising those terrible conditions?

utterances.speaker: VUJADIN POPOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mr. Nicholls, when he says five to seven people per square metre, I know very well when we learned at school, at demonstrations, how many people can fit in a square metre, three to four. Five to seven is simply impossible. And I'm telling you, in that hall there were no more than 2 00 to 300 people because they were walking around the hall. And I know there were problems with water, and I said that big canisters should be provided and water distributed because the water-supply was off at the hall. It was summertime. There was some problem with the water-supply, so I ordered water to be provided. And I'm telling you it's not true that there were more than 2- to 300 people. I have no reason to lie and I'm not -- I have no reason to exaggerate the numbers.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Well, I'll let that pass. You realise that the people held in the Rocevic school, the ones you just admitted you were dealing with and deciding how much water they should get, were executed at Kozluk; you know that, right, on the 15th?

utterances.speaker: VUJADIN POPOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I learned that.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: And you know that over a thousand people were murdered at Kozluk and they all came out of that gym?

utterances.speaker: VUJADIN POPOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I am telling you again and I can swear before any god, there were no more than 2- to 300 people in the hall. There's no question of 500 or a thousand. I formed a convoy of 30 buses, one trailer-truck, and one longer bus. So many people cannot fit in that number of vehicles. 100 buses would be needed, and there's no reason to inflate anything.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Well, you keep saying -- and I have to put this to you. You keep saying you have no reason to lie. You've been sentenced to life in prison. You don't have much to lose by coming here with a whole new story that puts you as an innocent bystander at virtually every detention and execution site, do you?

utterances.speaker: VUJADIN POPOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Precisely for that reason I want to tell the truth, that things are not so black and white as they are represented.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Let's finish up the 14th. And talking about presenting the truth, at your trial, for the 14th of July in the afternoon, you presented a false alibi to cover up your participation, direct participation, in the Orahovac executions. Do you remember that you called Gordan Bjelanovic as your witness? Do you remember calling him? He's your alibi witness for --

utterances.speaker: VUJADIN POPOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: He couldn't even keep his story straight about where he was during the week of 9 to 15 July, do you remember that? That was at T 22094 in your trial, where Judge -- the honourable Presiding Judge in that case, Judge Agius asked your alibi witness: "But when you made the statement to Mr. Petrusic," which conflicted with the statement he made for you, "did you lie to him, when you said that you were near Potocari on the 12th of July? And if you did, why? What interest did you have to lie to him?" The witness gave a completely incoherent answer: "No, I did not lie. When I used to come there with General Krstic because ... I used to go to Vlasenica but not only in his car and not only General Krstic, and I know that I was bringing some pills, not with his car. We used to come with another car. So it's not like that day --" And then he trailed off. And the Trial Chamber in your case, paragraphs 1114 and 1115, found that. "... Bjelanovic's uncertainty about times and dates, the Trial Chamber finds that Bjelanovic's testimony does not raise a reasonable doubt that Popovic was in the Zvornik area on 14 July." And that's true, isn't it, you provided a completely false alibi in your case that didn't work?

utterances.speaker: VUJADIN POPOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: What you have just put, I don't understand half of it. There's one date, 12th, 14th, then back to 13th. I don't remember really everything that this gentleman, Bjelanovic, stated. But I know that on the 14th I was up there. And if he was uncertain about the date, it's quite normal after so many years had passed. And after all, it was not my intention to put forward a false witness. My Defence team was the only one that didn't do things like that.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Let's move on to the 15th of July now, the next day. And in paragraph 58 of your statement, you talk about going to the 10th Sabotage Detachment base in Dragasevac with Dragomir Pecanac. He asked you to accompany him. You sit and wait in the car for 10 to 15 minutes and do nothing, and then you leave. Then following on on your statement, paragraph 59, you go to Sekovici to see your brother, the vet. You go -- agree to meet in a restaurant in Lovnica. You go to the restaurant. Your brother doesn't show up so you just have lunch. Then you go back to the Drina Corps command. Now, unless my memory is very -- unless I'm mistaken, you didn't call your brother in your case, did you, to come up with an alibi for the 15th, that you were wandering around Lovnica by yourself, waiting for your brother to show up for lunch?

utterances.speaker: VUJADIN POPOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Why would I call my brother to testify to my alibi if we had a witness who said that on that day, around that time, he told me -- he saw me outside, and Pecanac was there for a while and after that he left. And second, I know -- I can imagine what you would have to say if only I had called my brother. There would be even more talk about false alibis and false witnesses. That's why I didn't call him.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Well, I'm saying this is a false alibi because on the 15th of July, you want to find some way to say you weren't at Rocevic where you were seen on the day that the prisoners were taken from Rocevic and murdered; right?

utterances.speaker: VUJADIN POPOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Before that I'd like you to tell me who saw me there.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Just --

utterances.speaker: VUJADIN POPOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: So it's not correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Just so you know - and you know who saw you there - you can't ask me questions. Okay? I ask the questions, you answer them. It's not a conversation. Unfortunately, that's the way trials work. So let me tell you, though, I will tell you because that was my next point. This is at paragraph 1118 from your trial judgement. Srecko Acimovic, who I know you attack, but Srecko Acimovic testified they found that you were there at Rocevic asking for soldiers to carry out the executions on the 15th of July. And my -- I'm putting it to you that's exactly what you were doing.

utterances.speaker: VUJADIN POPOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Unbelievable. If I could have cheated the laws of physics, then at the time when I was at the Dragasevac, I could have been at the same time somewhere else with Srecko Acimovic. And Srecko Acimovic invoked two other witnesses to confirm it. Those witnesses came and said it's nonsense. They said they had seen a tall man near a Campagnola, whereas I was sitting in the Golf. They didn't mention Popovic. Those were the men who he invited to corroborate his testimony. And we can discuss the logics of his testimony.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: I won't -- I'm not talking about you going to Dragasevac to the 10th Sabotage base that morning. But according to your testimony, on the 15th of July, in the heart of the murder operation, right when the column of Muslims is heading towards Zvornik, you essentially have the whole first half of the day off, that's what your statement says, because you go on a trip to Dragasevac and sit in the car for 10 to 15 minutes and then you go for a long lunch with your brother who doesn't show up.

utterances.speaker: VUJADIN POPOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: What are you trying to say? A column is moving and then Popovic gets out and stops the column? There are other people who are doing their jobs. Popovic was doing his job. On that day he was at his office, doing his job. A man comes up. We go out for a drink to get some rest, and then we go on. I worked from Saturday to Tuesday sometimes until 1.00 or 2.00 a.m., many days in a row. Please.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: And I'm -- what I'm putting to you is on that day, the 15th, you were doing your job and your job was to make sure that all the prisoners in custody at Rocevic were killed?

utterances.speaker: VUJADIN POPOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mr. Nicholls, let's try to be a little logical in our discussion about the 15th. According to you, Popovic was twiddling his thumbs. There's no ammunition, no men, no vehicles. He doesn't know where the executions would take place and he came to do something. What kind of officer is he? What does he know? Who orders the ammunition? Who orders the trucks? Who indicates the place where the executions would take place? Srecko Acimovic. Let's just try to be a little bit logical and then everything will be easy.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Well, I'll move on, but since -- I may need a moment to bring it up, but there was very clear evidence, since you asked who ordered the ammunition, that crates of ammunition went from the Zvornik Brigade logistics department and were delivered to Rocevic on the 15th of July and they were then used to execute the prisoners. So it came right out of the Zvornik Brigade command, and I'll try to find the cite for that. Let's move on to the 16th of July. This is in paragraphs - you don't need to read them, I'm just saying for the Trial Chamber - 66 to 75 of your statement. And on the 16th of July, according to you, you were at the school, and we agree, you were at the school at Pilica that day with Colonel Beara; right?

utterances.speaker: VUJADIN POPOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Right.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: And even by your own statement, paragraph 63, which, again for the record, I don't accept, but according to your statement, this is a day after you've learned that all the prisoners who were at Orahovac, Rocevic, and Petkovci had been murdered; right? So the 16th of July, you're at the school in Pilica with Beara and you've been told by Trbic, according to you, that all the prisoners have been murdered from the day before; right?

utterances.speaker: VUJADIN POPOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That was on the evening of the 15th.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can I just ask for more precision. Is it said in the statement that all -- I can't find this term "all prisoners."

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: This is paragraph 63: "On this occasion Trbic" --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Mr. Nicholls is kindly asked to read a little more slowly, please, for the interpreters.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: My apologies. Paragraph 63 --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: It just says "prisoners." It neither says all nor part of the prisoners.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: No. But what it --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Shall we continue?

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: It does say "the prisoners."

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Well, let me just ask you that: Do you dispute that all the prisoners at Orahovac, Rocevic, and Petkovci had been executed, other than the few survivors who we know about? That's what Trbic, according to you, told you; right?

utterances.speaker: VUJADIN POPOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I learned that from Trbic on the evening of the 15th when I came to the command of the Zvornik Brigade.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Thank you. Now let's look at your story for the 16th of July. We already talked about you being at the school at Pilica. Paragraph 70 and 71 of your statement, you see corpses outside the school. Paragraph 70, you see the prisoners being put on buses. You hear about an escape of prisoners, this is in paragraph 71. So Beara tells you to go check that out, find out about it. Sorry, paragraph 70, not 71. And so you go to the 1st command. You ask a local man who's chopping wood if he's seen any strangers. You stop for a cup of coffee. You have a little rest. Then you go back to the school and you find out that Beara has gone to Pilica. So that's the Pilica school story; right? You show up there, knowing about the murder operation, see some dead bodies, and just kind of wander around for a bit, have a rest, have a cup of coffee, and then come back?

utterances.speaker: VUJADIN POPOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: And the question is?

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: That's correct, right, what I just summarised? That's what you do that day at the school?

utterances.speaker: VUJADIN POPOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, it's a rather liberal reinterpretation with a dose of irony. For the most part that's it, but it's your own very liberal reading.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Thank you. But for the most part it is it, you say. Then you go to Pilica and Beara's at the restaurant right across from the Pilica Dom or cultural centre. And there are prisoners held in the cultural centre, and Beara wants you to get the keys -- he wants the keys to the local commune building so he sends you to get them. You go to this person's house. He's not there. You wait for a while because his mother says he'll be back from work soon, and then she gives you the keys because you're being quite polite. This is all in paragraph 71. And then at that moment you hear a burst of gun-fire from the direction of the cultural centre. And you run back to the cultural centre after hearing this burst of gun-fire, and Beara tells you, he's in the restaurant: These drunken idiots killed the prisoners; right? That's what happened?

utterances.speaker: VUJADIN POPOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: VUJADIN POPOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: But again, I can say you are reading it the same way you did before.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Now, the scene at the Pilica Dom, which just so you know -- well, you do know because it happened in your case, but also in this case the honourable Trial Chamber has been to the Pilica Dom, just so you know. Let me describe the scene to you there at the Dom. And we have no survivors from that execution site that we know of, nobody survived, so there's no testimony I can read to you about the conditions. But this is what the clean-up crew described the scene as. This is Jevto Bogdanovic in this case, 92 bis, P00385 at e-court pages 16 to 23, describing the scene inside, the bodies. "Well, some were curled up, some were stretched out. There was this huge pile and they were piled up, one over the other. They were dead. "Q. Were you drinking ... that day to sustain yourself? "A. Yes. We did." And he says they were drinking rakija. "Q. Where did you get that? "A. Neighbours, the locals, brought it -- that to us. We drank for courage, to be able to sustain looking at the blood and the bodies and the brains of the people." Now, he and the other members of his workers' platoon, according to the evidence in your case, loaded the bodies onto two trucks, two truckloads of bodies come out of the Pilica Dom. And loading the bodies, he said they worked from morning to 3.00 p.m. That's 22 of that case. And your trial judgement - the question is in a moment, I'm describing the scene to you in case you don't remember - paragraph 543, the Trial Chamber found that two tipper trucks were used and that inside the Pilica cultural centre there were corpses piled up on each other, lying scattered all over the place. Two truckloads of corpses, and your story is that you heard a burst of fire?

utterances.speaker: VUJADIN POPOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm sorry, maybe you didn't read it well. I heard bursts of fire. It was not one or a burst of fire. It was firing that lasted for several minutes, 10 to 15, 10 for sure. So bursts of fire was rather what I said. How it was translated to you, that's something I wouldn't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Well, what your statement says at paragraph 22 is: "At that moment, a burst of gun-fire was heard from the direction of the cultural centre." Well, you tell me, if you've got -- if you've got 500 men crammed into the Pilica Dom, you were there, how long does it take to shoot 500 men?

utterances.speaker: VUJADIN POPOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: How would I know how long it takes? I did not make the norms. Never in my life did I, that's why -- but you're not right when you say -- that you say that from paragraph 79. I will read it out to you from my statement which I believe to be authoritative. It says: "Bursts of fire were heard at the moment." That's how it reads in my version, not "a burst of fire." As the men were crowded --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Just a second.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] 72 --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, it's 72.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Shall we upload the -- both versions.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: And, Your Honours, I'll accept that possibly it says "bursts." It doesn't change my cross a whole lot so we don't need to spend too much time on it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Very well. Then let's continue.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Your Honour, Mr. Popovic has a question.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, if you would allow, it has been quoted again wrongly. It doesn't say "bursts of fire," but it says "bursting fire," that's what it literally says. There is no limitation. It wasn't a burst of fire, but it was firing coming in bursts, which denotes that it came from a number of weapons.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Okay --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Just a second. I said to upload the document a minute ago but it's not there still. Okay. Let's continue.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: All right. And maybe we should have it because I'm going to continue reading from paragraph 72 in a minute.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Your statement, I'm reading the English, Mr. Popovic, you say: "We were surprised because we did not know who was shooting in a populated area. I went outside to see what was happening and went towards the restaurant from which we had come. In the restaurant I found Beara who told me, 'These drunken idiots killed the prisoners.'" So I'll go back to my question. You've clarified it wasn't just a burst. You were there. How long did it take to kill all 500 men in the Pilica Dom? How long were people shooting those prisoners?

utterances.speaker: VUJADIN POPOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mr. Nicholls, I really don't know for how long they were shooting, but I know that it wasn't a single burst of fire. It was heavy firing from automatic weapons which lasted for some time. And I think that to the best of my recollection perhaps one grenade may have been thrown. I don't know. But that was certainly that.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: I was just going to ask you about grenades, but you've confirmed that you heard at least one grenade. Now, I have a little -- I won't comment. How is it that you're at a mass execution site, if we're to believe you, you're innocent and have nothing to do with it, and you can't remember how long it took to kill these 500 men? You would think you would remember how long. I think you're minimising -- you're minimising the time because you were there. You were there while they killed 500 men.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Objection.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, no, no.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Mr. Karadzic.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Objection. The witness is not defending himself. He is stating what he knows.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: It's not a proper intervention. Do you remember the question, Mr. Popovic?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I would like Mr. Nicholls to repeat it, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: I'm going to ask you again. I'm putting it to you you're minimising or being wishy-washy on how long it took to kill these men because you were there and so you don't want it to be a long time when you could have done something about it. You're -- what you're saying is that you hear the gun-fire and you rush back and by then it's all over, and you're saying that because you're there at the execution site. That's why I'm asking you: How long did it take to kill all those men? How long did you hear bursts of gun-fire for?

utterances.speaker: VUJADIN POPOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: To answer you, I really did not look at my watch, but those bursts of fire, the firing certainly lasted for 10 or 15 minutes. I was not at the very location. I came to the cafe restaurant and that was why I asked: What happened? And he said: The drunken idiots that we had found there -- they had already been drunk. I can even describe one who was swaying on his feet next to the bar and he had an M84 machine-gun. So he said: Those drunken idiots killed them, and that's it. I'm not defending, I'm not minimising in any way. I just remember about this grenade. Was it one or two? I don't know. But I remember that there was a detonation.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Okay. Well, from the places we do have survivors from, Orahovac execution site, Kravica execution site, we know and the pattern is that it's very hard to kill 500 or a thousand men all in one go. So at those execution sites -- and, excuse me, Branjevo, what happened is after the bursts of fire, somebody had to walk around shooting the remaining living prisoners and killing the ones who had survived. So while you were at the Pilica Dom restaurant right across the street, who was going around shooting the survivors? Or how were the survivors killed?

utterances.speaker: VUJADIN POPOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I suppose that those who had shot were doing this. I don't suppose that an officer went out and went around, but those who had been shooting anyway, they went there and then finished it off. I don't have a different answer to that.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: And were you having a coffee or a beer or a rakija in the restaurant while these unknown soldiers were finishing it off? Because your statement doesn't say: After I heard these bursts of fire and came back, I heard isolated shots, or anything like that.

utterances.speaker: VUJADIN POPOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mr. Nicholls, a statement can never contain everything. You might recollect something later on, but I told you the main things. I can suppose that they finished the task that they had. But whether we were drinking coffee or beer at that time, I really wasn't drinking. Some people did and they were half drunk, if not completely drunk.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Okay. Now, just like Kravica, if we're to believe your story that you're not part of this, what do you do to go into that Dom and try to get medical help for any survivors? What did you do to try to save anybody there if you were innocent and not part of this? Nothing, right?

utterances.speaker: VUJADIN POPOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: VUJADIN POPOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: But maybe I could explain a little. I did not try -- because, look, when you are in the presence of your superior, then usually you look at what your superior is doing. He assumes the responsibility, and it would turn out that I was acting as if I was his superior and taking initiative on myself. The one who is the superior assumes complete responsibility. At the moment I simply didn't -- it was also a moment of shock, and at this moment I simply couldn't, when he was there, take any initiative.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: And just to be very clear for our record, when you say "he," you mean Colonel Beara?

utterances.speaker: VUJADIN POPOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Okay. Let's look at some of the evidence from the trial about you on this day.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Could I have P05077.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: You know all about these from your trial, no surprises. This is the intercept of your conversations that day. Not your conversations, I apologise, conversations about you. All right. This is 16 July 1995, 1358 hours. Zlatar, who we can agree is Zvornik Brigade, duty officer calling Palma -- sorry, Zlatar, Drina Corps, speaking with Palma, Zvornik Brigade. And Palma, Zvornik Brigade, calls and says: "Hello ... give me the duty officer. "A. Yes? "Palma duty officer speaking. 500 litres of D2 /diesel fuel/ for Lieutenant-Colonel Popovic. Drina Corps: "For Lieutenant-Colonel Popovic? "Yes." I don't have that much time so I'll try to move through this quite quickly. If we go further down, after the line disconnects, we see the second conversation, again between Drina Corps and Zvornik Brigade. "Hello! Is that Basevic? "Yes, it is. "The guys at Zlatar didn't understand well. I asked for the duty officer, you know? "Yes. "Lieutenant-Colonel Popovic is here at Palma, you know? "What? "Popovic is at Palma. "Yes. "500 litres of D2 are urgently being asked for him or else the work he's doing will stop." Basevic: "Well, fuck him, don't you have 500 litres of oil? They're asking for 2 tonnes loaded. "Well, I don't know. He just called me from the field. He told me to pass the message over to you." If we can go over to the next page. And I'll go to the third conversation here. "Give me the operations duty officer. Is Major Golic there by chance? "Yes." That's Pavo Golic, right, Mr. Popovic, Pavo Golic is at Drina Corps?

utterances.speaker: VUJADIN POPOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Majo Golic, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: "Golic, Pop just called and told me to contact you. 500 litres of D2 have to be sent to him immediately, otherwise his work will stop. "500 litres or else his work will stop. Go on right away. "... a bus loaded with oil is to go to Pilica village. That's it. "500 litres." And then they talk about the tank. So on the 16th of July, you're in Zvornik Brigade AOR and you're requesting 500 litres of D2. And before I ask you the question about it, let's just look at the duty officer notebook which also refers to this same conversation.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: That's P04585, e-court page 81 in the Serbian, 82 in the English, and it needs to be the second translation of the duty officer notebook if that makes sense.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] May I just ask the learned Mr. Nicholls, I do not want to meddle, but I'm afraid that perhaps too many elements may accumulate in one question. Perhaps he could deal with them one by one.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes --

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: I think it will be a very simple question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, let's deal with these intercepts first. We'll come back to the duty officer's log-book.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: All right.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Well, what these intercepts show, don't they, Mr. Popovic, is that that day, 16 July --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Shall we go back to the intercept.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Yes, sorry. 05077 is the intercept.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: While it's coming up, you've read this intercept many times for your trial. Zvornik Brigade duty officer, who we say is Trbic at this time, is calling Palma saying that you've requested 500 litres of D2 or your work will stop at 2.00 and it needs to go to Pilica. Your story is that you're kind of tagging around behind Beara in Pilica, not really doing anything. Why do you need 500 litres of D2 fuel while you're in Pilica on the 16th?

utterances.speaker: VUJADIN POPOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, let's explain now. It's obvious from this conversation that the duty operations officer is asking for 500 litres of fuel in my name. Now, I wonder if I called the duty officer and told him that, I would have had to call the communications centre in the Zvornik Brigade and ask for the duty operations officer. As soon as I got in touch with the communications centre in the Zvornik Brigade, I could have in the same manner called the communications centre of the Drina Corps, because that was the man I needed, and ask for the oil. I claim that somebody was asking for the oil in my name. I certainly didn't need it, and later on we'll see where it was used. Because to request something and not to use it, why?

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Well --

utterances.speaker: VUJADIN POPOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Where was it poured? When did it arrive?

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: So you don't dispute the authenticity of this intercept? You're saying somebody else called in your name, but you don't dispute that this is an authentic intercept of a phone conversation that day?

utterances.speaker: VUJADIN POPOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, in essence, we tried to show that it was not valid when we presented our defence. What I deny is that I was requesting that personally in my name. Why would I take the longer route when I could have taken the more direct one, and when I was supposed to go up to Parlog I called directly the duty operations officer. Why wouldn't I have called directly in this case? I think that someone used a bit of -- we'll see in the end where it was poured, who received this oil.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Now could we go to the duty officer notebook, please, unless Your Honours have questions about the intercept. So e-court page 82 of the English of the second translation, that's correct, and 81 of the Serbian.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: All right. Zvornik Brigade duty officer notebook for 16th of July, same day as the intercept, 1400 hours is written there, two minutes after the intercept we just looked at. It states: "At 1400 hours Popovic requested a bus with a full tank and 500 litres of D2" --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Just a second. Is it the correct page in B/C/S?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It's not here.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: No. It's ERN 02935766, so three pages earlier in the Serbian.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Oh, no, sorry, 66. My mistake.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: That's right.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: So, Mr. Popovic, what was written in the duty officer notebook on the 16th of July, that you -- it says: "... Popovic requested a bus with a full tank and 500 litres of D2 ..." And then just as we saw in the intercept, it says: "... Zlatar duty officer and Golic informed."

utterances.speaker: VUJADIN POPOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I do not deny that that is what it says here, but I really wonder, why would I need a bus with a full tank? And another thing, I repeat once again, I did not request the fuel, I personally. What would I use it for?

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Well, what you would use it for is transporting --

utterances.speaker: VUJADIN POPOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: -- and murdering the Muslims in Pilica and Branjevo that day, bringing them from the school where you were that day, you admit, to Branjevo Farm and murdering them. You were using that fuel for the murder operation. That's what you would use the fuel for, what you were found guilty for.

utterances.speaker: VUJADIN POPOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mr. Nicholls, to the best of my recollection, as I remember some of the statements, the transport of prisoners from the school in Pilica was finished around after 2.00. And when the fuel arrived, who needed it then? And another thing, Mr. Nicholls, it's visible, and you showed it from vehicle work logs of machines, that they were filled up with fuel at their own gas stations. And thirdly, if these buses, if their tanks were filled with this fuel, then the vehicle logs would have to include this information, that their tanks were filled, because otherwise they would have to show what they did with it. You said, I think yourself, that it was black gold for us. And here it seems: Well, you use up 500 litres, never mind, just give it to me. So there are vehicle work logs, both for the buses and for construction machines. So we can look at that and then check if it's true what you are claiming.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: P04669, please, quickly, before the break.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Shall we deal with it after a break?

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Of course, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes. The Chamber will have a break till 11.00.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Tieger.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Excuse me --

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Sorry.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: I know the Court wishes to break now, so I will defer my comments, but I wish to be heard on a courtesy copy of a motion for leave to reply which we received before the Court considers that. I can do that at the beginning of the next session.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: I would like to hear you now.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Certainly. Let me begin by noting that I once noted to this Court that the nature of direct cross and re-direct examination normally result in a funnel process, and that in the hands of the accused, it often was ballooned into an elaborate reversal of that. Same thing is happening here and we object to that. In this instance, the Defence claims that it's the Prosecution which is conflating parliamentary privilege and parliamentary immunity with the latter of which he asserts is inapplicable. Our response to the motion was based on the materials and provisions that he provided in his motion which indeed included lengthy annexes on parliamentary immunity. Even more specifically in paragraph 5 he states: "Similar provisions for non-liability of statements made by members of parliament exist in virtually every country in the world," which is an implicit reference to an immunity and, indeed, the footnote at the end of that sentence refers to provisions on parliamentary immunity. So any alleged "conflation" of privilege and immunity is his own doing and he should not be permitted to attempt to rectify those errors in a reply. Secondly, he wants to make submissions on the universality of parliamentary privilege in civil and common law jurisdictions, but he already argued in paragraph 5 of his motions that such provisions for non-liability allegedly exist in virtually every country of the world, and this is not a new issue. He should not be able to supplement his submissions and thus gain the last word in the fashion that we constantly see and that I think the Court has discouraged. And finally, I would note that whatever Mr. Krajisnik has communicated to him concerning his intention to invoke some privilege is irrelevant to the issue of Karadzic's standing. And those -- that's the information I wanted to provide with respect to that. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: The Chamber will have a break till 11.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Robinson.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBINSON
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. I'd just like to introduce to the Chamber Kathryn Heslop, who is a lawyer from Perth in Australia who has been assisting our team as pro bono legal assistant. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you. I apologise for the delay. The Chamber wanted to make some photocopies of documents, but the copy machine was out of order and that took a while. The Chamber thought it important to resolve the issue regarding the motion to preclude questioning of Krajisnik on statement made in parliament before he comes to testify. But before we go on, I have to note a couple of things. First, the Chamber notes that a motion such as this should not be filed a mere two days before the start of the witness's testimony. The Prosecution had to respond within a day, putting an unnecessary strain on its resources which should have been avoided, given that Mr. Krajisnik has been listed on the accused's Rule 65 ter list since August 2012. And secondly, as to the substance of the motion, the Chamber is disappointed that the accused would think that requesting the serious relief sought in the motion it would be sufficient to present such a poorly argued motion as this one, without even attempting to demonstrate in which manner this purported privilege applies in international criminal proceedings. However, having said that, in light of the subject matter, the Chamber decided that it would be helpful to hear the parties. In that sense, the Chamber will allow the Defence to reply and we'll hear you orally now.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBINSON
utterances.text: Very good, Mr. President. I'm ready to do that. Mr. President, we can start with the English Bill of Rights from 1689, that says that the freedom of speech and debates of proceedings in parliament ought not to be impeached or questioned in any court or place out of parliament. Then we have the United States Constitution, Article 1 -- excuse me, Article 1, Section 6, that says that for any speech or debate in either House, they shall not be questioned in any place. And it's our position that that parliamentary privilege or Speech and Debate Clause privilege as we call it in the United States applies to the testimony -- the questioning of Mr. Krajisnik in this court. And as a member, indeed, president of the Assembly, both of Bosnia and Republika Srpska, he has the right not to be questioned about anything he said during proceedings in those bodies. I apologise for the way the issue was brought to your attention. It actually came up on Sunday evening when I met with Mr. Krajisnik and we filed it on Monday morning, as soon as we could possibly file it. I apologise that it wasn't well argued, but I hope that you can understand the point because I think it is a very important one and I think we're right about this. So, first of all, the Prosecution says that Dr. Karadzic has no standing to raise this. Well, Mr. Krajisnik, when he comes here, will assert the privilege that he has and so that's one basis for dealing with this issue. And it's our position also that Dr. Karadzic has the right under Rule 95 to have excluded any evidence whose admission would be antithetical to or would seriously damage the integrity of the proceedings. And we believe that for this Court, whether it be international or domestic, to require a member of parliament to justify or to be questioned about statements he made on the floor of that parliament would be antithetical to and seriously damage the integrity of these proceedings. Now, the Prosecution says that Dr. Karadzic has waived the privilege, but Dr. Karadzic can't waive Mr. Krajisnik's privilege, neither can another witness, such as President Dodik who came here and testified about his statements in parliament and was willing to do so. So there's no waiver that can preclude the operation of the parliamentary privilege. Neither has Mr. Krajisnik by testifying in his own case waived his right to later claim that privilege in other proceedings, just as a witness or suspect who's questioned by the Prosecution before the trial can't be called to repeat those statements or questioned about those statements in violation of his privilege against self-incrimination at a trial --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Did he not testify in the Popovic case?

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes, he did. Although I don't know that he testified about his statements. But in any event, this is a privilege, like many other privileges, that can be asserted at any time. For example, a war correspondent in the Brdjanin case published an article about the very thing that he was to be questioned about, yet claimed the privilege successfully during the Brdjanin case against being compelled to testify about that very same topic. There's no authority for the proposition that the Prosecution indicates that parliamentary immunity or parliamentary privilege is limited to domestic proceedings. Other privileges, such as that of the International Committee for the Red Cross, the war correspondent privilege, the lawyer/client privilege, the physician/patient privilege, and even the penitent/clergy privilege are all recognised in international tribunals, whether it be this one or the International Criminal Court. Now, it's true that in international tribunals the immunity from prosecution of a head of state or a member of parliament may not necessarily apply, as in the case of President Taylor, President Milosevic, and others. But this is not an immunity that's being asserted; this is an evidentiary privilege. And the question before the Chamber is whether this evidentiary privilege ought to be respected or disregarded. The materials that we appended to our motion show that this privilege is almost universally accepted, not only in common law countries like the United Kingdom, the United States, Australia, and Canada, but even in civil law countries that came out of the French Revolution as one of our documents show.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: I'm sorry to interrupt. Could you tell us what that privilege is like in actual terms? Does it mean that we cannot use the transcript or the record of the parliament debate at all?

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBINSON
utterances.text: No, not at all. No. That may have been an issue that could have been raised by Mr. Krajisnik in his own case, whether materials that -- things that he said could be used -- introduced against him. What we're talking about in this case, in this context is a much more narrower part of the privilege which is that -- a privilege not to be questioned in a court about what you've said. So we don't ask that a statement that [overlapping speakers] --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: So we have no difficulty using Krajisnik's words in the parliament?

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBINSON
utterances.text: We can --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: In written -- as written evidence?

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBINSON
utterances.text: That's correct. As long as he's not questioned about that, then I don't think in this context the privilege is violated by admitting it against Dr. Karadzic. But if it were to be a trial of Mr. Krajisnik, it might be a different situation, but we don't have to deal with that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: I'm waiting for the ... Yes, I was waiting for the translation. What's the effect of that privilege in actual terms? Take the privilege against self-incrimination. The witness is entitled to invoke his privilege not to testify against his self-incrimination, notwithstanding that, the Chamber in international tribunal has the power to compel the witness to answer the question with certain caveats.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes, that's because the -- then it's no longer incriminating because it can't be used, so it's no longer -- the privilege against self-incrimination is -- no longer comes into play in the sense that the statements are not being used against the person. Now, I don't know of any other privilege --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: I wanted to compare those two kinds of privilege, how is it -- how are they different from each other.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yeah, that's a good question. And I don't know of any other privilege that can be overcome in that way. For example, you couldn't compel a person who had a lawyer/client communication to reveal -- you couldn't compel the lawyer to reveal that communication or you couldn't compel a physician. You couldn't compel the ICRC to come in here and give evidence if it was stated that it wouldn't be made public, for example, or you couldn't compel a war correspondent if the qualifications for the privilege existed to give evidence with the assurance that it wouldn't be made known to those in the field that he had given that evidence. So I think self-incrimination is a special thing in which immunity -- a use immunity essentially overcomes that privilege, but I'm not sure in any other context that it can be done.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MORRISON
utterances.text: Just for future research, and I'm working just from memory here, I think it would be worth looking at the provisions of the Criminal Justice Act of 2003 in the United Kingdom and the dicta of Lord Mustill in Regina versus Director of Serious Fraud Office, I think, Ex parte Smith 1992. There Lord Mustill made some very cogent observations.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBINSON
utterances.text: Very well. I will do that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Still we do not have the copy of your motion so that's why I'm asking you this question. Could you define the privilege as it is provided in the Statute. What is it like?

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBINSON
utterances.text: Okay. I'm -- we're -- this is a very, very narrow application of the privilege. There's a lot of litigation over peripheral parts of this privilege, whether an aide to a congressman or to a parliament member can refuse to -- can invoke the privilege, whether it includes acts --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Could you read out the provision of the Statute or whatever.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes. First --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Definition.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes. "... the freedom of speech and debates or proceedings in Parliament ought not to be impeached or questioned in any court or place out of Parliament," that's the English Bill of Rights of 1689. And the Article 1, Section 6 of the United States Constitution, the relevant clause simply says: "... for any speech or debate in either House, they shall not be questioned in any other place." And just as an example, in the United States, the US Supreme Court dealt with this in 1972 in the case of Senator Mike Gravel who had read parts of the Pentagon Papers into the record during Senate proceedings, and a Federal Grand Jury was convened in Washington DC to investigate aspects of his conduct. And the US Supreme Court held that Senator Gravel and more particularly his aide could not be questioned during the Grand Jury proceedings about anything he said on the floor of the Senate, even though he could be questioned about other aspects of how they published later the Pentagon Paper excerpts and things like that. So --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Was that not an issue of immunity?

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBINSON
utterances.text: No, that was an issue of testimonial privilege. So -- because the issue of immunity is separate. Whether -- at that time there was no prosecution. It was just questioning of a witness. That's the very narrow issue that we have in this case. We're not talking about immunity because the person asserting the privilege isn't on trial here. So we're just talking about whether a person can be questioned about what they said on the floor of a parliament or assembly. That's the only issue. And if I can just make the last point about customary international law, and that is that the customary international law exists to protect the rights of individuals and an accused so that rules aren't applied in an international tribunal that would be unfair because either they weren't in existence at the time or they're somehow being -- operating to the disadvantage of an accused and make a trial otherwise unfair. So it's to the Prosecution to show that customary international law allows for a witness to be questioned about the statements he made in parliament, not for the Defence to show that customary international law would prohibit such questioning. That concludes my reply, unless you have any questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Mr. Tieger, are you ready to respond to this or do you need some more time?

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: I'll respond very quickly and I would need more time. I think the Court's earlier point is a very fair one, and that is that it was raised inappropriately, argued perfunctorily, and now expanded on in the broadest of terms in a manner that handicaps the Prosecution obviously. But a couple of quick points, number one -- and reserving the right to respond further especially by those who have had an opportunity to research this a little more thoroughly. Number one, we still don't really know the extent of the privilege in domestic jurisdictions, much less in international usage. The Defence takes the broadest of provisions and then leaps forward hugely to simply adopt the most favourable interpretation to them. Number two, I'm glad Mr. Robinson used the word "conflation" before because that's precisely what he's doing now in connection with Mr. Krajisnik. He posits the situation where somebody is called upon by the Prosecution and then asked about statements made that supposedly are privileged, but what's happening here, in fact, is Mr. Krajisnik made lavish use of the Assembly session statements that he made and others made in his own case in his examination-in-chief. He even independently tendered and produced such sessions. Now that he's been unsuccessful in that effort and confronted by the totality of the statements made in those sessions, he now seeks to come here, testify about matters related to those -- to that previous testimony and to those statements in the -- that were made in the Assembly, and insulate himself from the truth-seeking process of cross-examination by hiding from the statements he made, even though he previously testified about them and even though he's testifying -- he purports to testify about matters that implicate those same statements. And finally --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Just a second. Yes, please continue.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Finally, Mr. President, in this initial submission, which I hope is more than sufficient, Mr. Robinson mentioned that Mr. Krajisnik was the president of the Bosnian Assembly and the president of the RS Assembly. The RS Assembly is no Assembly recognised by international law. What happens here, if you want to analogise to the marital privilege, is there was a marriage and he left it, and now he wants to have the same privilege applied to his new -- whatever he says to his new girlfriend.
