The RS Assembly was not recognised by any international body, and to assert an international privilege on the basis of a body that was formed by people who left an official body recognised by the international community established for the purpose of destroying that body is quite absurd. And on that basis alone, this should be rejected as inappropriate and frivolous.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Having not had enough time, it's difficult to follow your assertion that while we can use the transcript of the debate in the parliament can be -- can be used as evidence, but you cannot ask a question about that when the speaker, one of the speakers, came to testify. Further, Mr. Karadzic, the Defence itself has tendered a vast amount of parliamentary transcripts and also Mr. Karadzic elicited evidence from numerous participants himself. How do you reconcile this? It's difficult to follow.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBINSON
utterances.text: Well, Mr. President, let's say that you had someone who wished to invoke their right against self-incrimination, say even Mr. Krajisnik wanted to invoke his right against self-incrimination here, the fact that Dr. Karadzic had introduced many of his statements during the trial, would that mean that he wasn't given that privilege to invoke the self-incrimination privilege? Or the fact that he had testified at his own trial would still give him the right to at this trial invoke his privilege of self-incrimination. So I don't think that the fact that we have before us materials relating to the parliament sessions means that he is not able to invoke the privilege that he has not to be questioned about those in any court.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Do you have information that Mr. Krajisnik is going to invoke his privilege?

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes, definitely.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Tieger.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Well, just to note, Mr. President, that the invocation of any privilege, for example, the privilege against self-incrimination during a cross-examination, which effectively shields the witness from being cross-examined and the truth-seeking process from being perfected, may mean that the examination-in-chief has to be rejected also. Defence is aware of that and presumably takes that risk if in -- in pushing what I continue to claim is a frivolous motion.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BAIRD
utterances.text: Mr. Robinson, can I hear you on Mr. Tieger's point that the RS Assembly is no assembly recognised by international law, so therefore privilege wouldn't apply there at all.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. President, and Judge Baird. First of all, the laws of war and all the international regulations clearly apply to the officials of the RS, including their obligation to follow the Geneva Conventions and their obligations -- and their liabilities. That's why we're here. So the fact that the Republika Srpska Assembly is not recognised by some international body - I don't know who Mr. Tieger's referring to, perhaps the United Nations General Assembly or the United Nations Security Council - isn't determinative of whether this is a privilege that still applies to that body. I note that the privilege also applies to many other bodies not recognised by the United Nations, including the states of the United States. For example, in Kansas, a state legislator was able to successfully invoke this privilege in a case called People versus Neufeld, in which he was questioned about conduct that took place on the floor of the Kansas legislature. So you don't have to be an official sovereign body to have this privilege apply to you, at least in our contention.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BAIRD
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MORRISON
utterances.text: Mr. Robinson, this is obviously coming without opportunity for proper research. I've always understood the UK parliamentary privilege to be a form of immunity, and to make the distinction in those circumstances between immunity and privilege seems to be a rather artificial one. But my understanding is that that immunity only applies to defamation, contempt of court, and breaches of the Official Secrets Act.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBINSON
utterances.text: Actually, I've been spending a fair amount of time reading UK materials last night -- and I know you know it better than I do, but I think that's part of the difference between -- well, that's part of the confusion about immunity and privileges because they do refer to it in UK as parliamentary immunity. But I believe that that encompass -- that broad term encompasses this privilege against being questioned that's in the Bill of Rights. And I have noticed in several of the materials that I've read -- I can't say I've actually read cases. I've been reading treatises essentially, but they seem to say that that parliamentary immunity stems from the English Bill of Rights including the provision that I have read out.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Very well. The Chamber regards this motion at the moment as moot because it's not clear whether or not the Prosecution is going to put questions about those matters contained in the transcript of the parliament and it's not clear whether Mr. Krajisnik has -- is going to invoke his privilege at the moment. We'll deal with it when it arises. Having said that, should we bring in the witness, Mr. Popovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Excuse me, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Nicholls.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: I'm a little bit lost for when the next break would be, just for my timing of my remaining topics.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: We're going to have a break at 12.30 --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: -- as usual.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: If you'd like to have it earlier or later we'll --

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: No, that's fine. We started a few minutes late, I thought, so I wasn't sure if we were going longer.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: I take it we are not reaching Mr. Krajisnik today, just for planning purposes?

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBINSON
utterances.text: Actually, I think we are.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: We are?

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBINSON
utterances.text: I believe the Prosecution has about an hour and five or ten minutes left. So far we have very little re-direct, if any. So we did think that Mr. Krajisnik would be -- I just sent an e-mail that he should be ready at 1.30, but I may be optimistic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: But at least we are not going to reach the cross-examination of Mr. Krajisnik?

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBINSON
utterances.text: Definitely not.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Please continue, Mr. Nicholls.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. P04669, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Still on Pilica, Mr. Popovic, still on fuel. Another document you're familiar with from your trial.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: E-court page 67, please. This is P04669. That's what I'm looking -- there we go. Now, we already looked at the intercept. We already looked at the duty officer notebook, all of which said fuel for Popovic, Lieutenant-Colonel Popovic, in the intercepts. This is -- if we could have the Serbian. The Serbian is page 68, please, in the Serbian. Sorry, I didn't read that out before.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: I want to be very quick about this, Mr. Popovic. You've already explained your theory of why all these references to you and the fuel are somehow inaccurate. This is from the 16th of July. We see on the top row, second column, it's a materials list. It's got name, the address station handwritten in, this is on the right, in the second box down, in box 15, for Lieutenant-Colonel Popovic, that's you. And the amount, remarks, out of 500 litres of D2 fuel, 140 were returned. So 500 litres went out to you, just as requested in the intercept, just as noted in the duty officer notebook, just as you said it's a black gold, so the 140 litres that weren't used were returned. And you agree with me, on the right it says Captain S. Milosevic. Sreten Milosevic was a logistics officer in the Zvornik Brigade; correct?

utterances.speaker: VUJADIN POPOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I really don't know whether Sreten Milosevic -- I mean, I don't know him personally --

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Okay --

utterances.speaker: VUJADIN POPOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: -- I know from the statement that he gave that he was assistant for logistics, but I personally don't know him, that's for sure.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Thank you. You've answered the question. I'm putting it to you that this document shows exactly what I put to you with the other documents. You requested 500 litres of D2 fuel and it was sent to you.

utterances.speaker: VUJADIN POPOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: This document shows exactly what I was saying. See. If somebody is asking for something they had to send the material list in my name. Now, what is missing? What is crucial? That I received it. If it was sent to me, I'm the one who was supposed to receive it. It was received by some Bogicevic, Branko. I'm not Branko Bogicevic; I'm Vujadin Popovic. I was supposed to receive that. If I was not accessible then, let's say I wasn't accessible, then there's my command. They could have brought it on the second day, the third day, whatever, I would have signed it. No problem.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Okay. Try to be a little bit realistic here. Branko Bogicevic is the driver who delivered the fuel. You had him testify in your trial. That's why his name is there. It wasn't sent to him for his use; he's the driver.

utterances.speaker: VUJADIN POPOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: But that is the problem. He could not receive it. He's just a driver. I'm the one who was supposed to receive it because it was sent to me.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Your Honours, I'll --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Now, I don't know, what did he do with that? I can put the question in a justified way, what happened to this?

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: P05118, Your Honours, is the fuel log for Bogicevic. I'm not going to bring it up.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: But your own lawyer introduced that in your trial to show that the fuel was delivered to Pilica, although there was a story that unknown soldiers received it; right?

utterances.speaker: VUJADIN POPOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: As far as I can remember Mr. Bogicevic's testimony, he said that he brought that fuel there between 7.00 or 8.00, or perhaps even later, in the evening. He said that that fuel was poured out into canisters for some soldiers, and that's it.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Is this another frame-up of you that's taking place in July 1995, right in the middle of the murder operation, the duty officers in Zvornik are writing down in the notebook: Popovic requests 500 litres of D2, 500 litres of fuel? The intercepts say Popovic need 500 litres of fuel or his work will stop. Are those fabrications? Is that what you're saying?

utterances.speaker: VUJADIN POPOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's what the document says. I'm not saying that, but that's what the document says in this statement of this man. I have to admit something to you, it happened sometimes that I would ask for something and not get it and then all right. And then if you would say it was ordered by the commander, then all of a sudden you could get it. These are little tricks that we all resorted to. That's the way it was.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Now, there's no combat in Pilica on the --

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Sorry, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Was this document, the fuel receipt, not admitted on its own?

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: The basis for its admission I have to wait a moment. I don't know if it was a bar table or other --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: This document is a part of the - what was the name? - intercept authentication binder, Stefanie --

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Oh, yes. Yes, Your Honour, it was in there. That's correct.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: -- Frease, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Yes, you're correct.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: It's included there?

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: It is, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Not tendered separately?

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: No, I don't believe so, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you. Yes, please continue.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: When you were in Pilica on the 16th of July, there was no combat going on; right? No pitched battle with the 28th Division?

utterances.speaker: VUJADIN POPOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Thank you. Bisina, I'm going to ask you -- talk to you about Bisina.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: This is in paragraphs, just for Your Honours' reference, 85 to 88 of his statement.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: You admit to being present at Bisina at the site of the mass killing in paragraph 88. You admit that you told the soldiers there, unknown soldiers according to you, to bury the bodies of the victims. At paragraph 89. And your story is that, just like Orahovac, just like Rocevic, just like you just explained for Pilica, you're just there, fourth execution site in a row, as a kind of innocent bystander; right?

utterances.speaker: VUJADIN POPOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mr. Nicholls, how would you be reacting if I did not have a document filled out in handwriting for the Golf, the work order? Vlasenica, Zvornik, Vlasenica, in the morning, that's what's written there. I really don't know -- well, God almighty, as they say, told me to write down that actual route. Usually we didn't record the routes, but this way you can see that I left. So yes, I cannot say: Yes, I filled out the travel authorisation, said that I would be going to Zvornik, and I went to Vienna. No. I cannot be in two different places at the same point in time. Quite simply, I cannot.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Let me be clear, is the story changing? Because what your statement says in paragraph 88 is that Bisina, you were there and when you got there there were the bodies of 30 people you saw. Were you at Bisina or not on 23rd of July?

utterances.speaker: VUJADIN POPOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I was, but I'm telling you about that morning when I went there. You want to present this as me being there all the time, being in attendance, and so on. But that's not true. That's the problem. So I'm trying to say that this part of my statement is correct. That's it. As for Bisina, I was there and I wrote that very nicely.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Now, you've just explained that you were there and talked about that morning. In your own trial on cross-examination by your lawyer, a credible witness said he was sure you were there at Bisina before the executions actually started. That's PW172, I'm giving the cite from the Popovic case, 10 March 2009, T 32585, lines 12 to 19. This is the questioning by Mr. Zivanovic. "Q. Could you tell me, please, you said that in that specific situation you approached Popovic at one point when it was all over and you asked him what you asked him. I won't repeat that. Can you tell me exactly, are you sure that you saw Popovic before this execution happened? Are you completely sure about that? "A. There in that very spot? "Q. Up there in Bisina, where it was happening, that's what I mean. "A. Yes, I'm sure."

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Can we go into private session for one moment, please, Your Honours?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I'm sorry.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: We are in open session, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Could I have P006 --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Are you moving away from this topic?

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: No. I was going to show another document.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Okay. Mr. Popovic, I didn't understand what you just said in private session. What you said you didn't re-dug this grave because -- because of what? Could you repeat your answer again.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: And could the witness please speak into the microphone.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Just a second. Come closer to the microphone, please.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, it's not that I didn't allow it. It's that I didn't order any grave relocation. I was saying that if I had felt guilty because I had done what Mr. Nicholls is saying, it would be expected that I should try to hide that grave. However, it remained intact. It's the only grave where the bodies were properly laid in. You can see that from the record of exhumations. All the other graves were dug up and relocated.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: I'm not sure I understood you. You didn't cover the so-called reburial or relocation of bodies in your statement. Were you involved in that reburial?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Not personally, Your Honours. I only controlled the use of fuel. I was asked to keep tabs on the use of fuel, but I did not participate directly.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: But you tried to keep that Bisina grave intact; is that -- was that your evidence?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, I'm saying if I had wanted to, when the reburials were done, I was aware they were being done, I could have asked them to relocate also the grave in Bisina, but I didn't do it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Then all the graves that had been dug out for reburial, did you do that to hide your responsibility then?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, I was not involved in that. I'm telling you, I just kept tabs on the use of fuel. That went down the chain of command and, of course, it was the security command that controlled this process. I personally did not take part in it. I didn't even know where some graves that were dug up later were located because it was some sort of secret. You cannot keep it completely secret if you're driving through towns. I would have been much happier if it hadn't been done at all. I don't know who ordered it, with what purpose. I mean, I know. We all know who has the right to give orders.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Back to you, Mr. Nicholls.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Thank you. And I'll come back to this a bit, Your Honour. I just ask some other questions first. P0663, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: All right. Now, this is the -- Mr. Popovic, this is kind of the counterpart -- well, I won't say that. This is another -- this is a document of a vehicle log, again by a Drina Corps driver, and it's also related to Bisina. If you look at page 2 in both languages, please, we see on the 23rd of July, Vlasenica, Sekovici, Bisina, Sekovici, eight people carried. And on the right, it's -- I'm not saying it's your signature, but on the right, far right, if we look at the English, it says "Popovic." And the testimony was -- I'm sorry, let me move back. The clear testimony from the driver of this vehicle log is that he went to Dragasevac, picked up some soldiers, brought them to Bisina, and then they killed the prisoners. And your name, Lieutenant-Colonel Popovic, is written there because it was your operation.

utterances.speaker: VUJADIN POPOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. It's my signature, yes. I won't deny it. It's my signature, but this signature on a vehicle log, I remember this well, this vehicle log was brought to my desk and I signed at once for all these days. You can see the same pen is used because there were some previous drives for the police before that. Maybe the police person in charge was absent so they brought it to me and I signed it, no problem, for three, four, five days. You can see that it's the same pen --

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Okay --

utterances.speaker: VUJADIN POPOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: -- I signed them all at the same time.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Right. So this van goes to Dragasevac -- remind us, please, tell the Chamber which unit had its base in Dragasevac in July of 1995? Which soldiers of which unit stayed in Dragasevac?

utterances.speaker: VUJADIN POPOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: There were members of the 10th Sabotage Detachment in Dragasevac.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: 10th Sabotage Detachment, persons with 10th Sabotage Detachment insignia carried out these executions. This truck, the driver said, he picked up soldiers at Dragasevac and took them to the execution site. You -- is your story that it's a coincidence that you signed off without -- you know, just signing documents, you didn't -- you sign off by coincidence on the vehicle log for the driver who brought the shooters to Bisina?

utterances.speaker: VUJADIN POPOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm telling you again, look, look at the dates. Look at all the dates I signed off for at the same time. I signed off for the 19th, 20th, 21st -- no, no, 21st is somebody else. Then 23rd, once, twice, thrice. I didn't even look at the routes I was signing off. I just signed them.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Okay. Your statement is a bit funny on this point because, from my understanding of it, you get a telephone call that unknown persons picked up the prisoners at Susica and took them to Bisina. That's in paragraph 86. Unknown men came and picked up the prisoners. That's not right. We have the vehicle log. We know exactly who picked up the prisoners. Drina Corps picked up the prisoners, right, from the Drina Corps prison in a Drina Corps bus -- truck.

utterances.speaker: VUJADIN POPOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mr. Nicholls, the officer on duty said that those people were unknown to him. And to me. Why would I have to know members of the 10th Sabotage Detachment who have absolutely no connection to me? I didn't know those soldiers personally. I knew their commander, only one person, and I knew who -- whose command they were under, and I knew I couldn't take them until they received proper orders. That's why they came from the forward command post because I had no right to command over them.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Transcript.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] On page 63, line 15, the witness said: "I signed them for them to justify the use of fuel." "To justify the use of fuel" is missing from the record. It would be a good idea if the witness could speak more slowly.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Do you confirm that, Mr. Popovic?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, yes. That's exactly it.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Paragraph 58 of your statement you say you go to Dragasevac to the 10th Sabotage base. What do you mean you don't know these soldiers? Is that why your statement says you wait in the car?

utterances.speaker: VUJADIN POPOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Certainly, that was the statement of the person who saw me in that car. I came to Dragasevac, waited for Pecanac in the car. Pecanac was shouting at those people, why were they asleep, why didn't they wake up. There was no officer on duty. I saw it was a complete ruckus. I didn't even want to go into the building. The man was himself standing outside.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Right. I wasn't going to do this, but let's look at paragraph 58. You can look at yours. This is your story on 15 July: "On the morning of 15 July 1995, I went to my office at the Drina Corps command in Vlasenica. Dragomir Pecanac from the VRS Main Staff came to see me at some point between 9.00 and 10.00 in the morning. He asked me to accompany him to Dragasevac. I set off in my car. Pecanac went to the building where members of the 10th Sabotage Detachment were housed. I remained in my car for about 10 to 15 minutes, and then I left." So your story is: Pecanac comes to you, says: Come with me to Dragasevac and then sit in your car while I go inside and yell at the 10th Sabotage for a bit and then you can go home. You're there for no purpose whatsoever. That's what your statement says.

utterances.speaker: VUJADIN POPOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, that's not at all what's in my statement. When Pecanac came to me see, I was in my office. I remember I was doing something. Maybe I was viewing a videotape, I cannot remember exactly, but I was doing my normal everyday work. Since we had known each other since Knin, we were good friends, we went everywhere together, he said: Come on, bro, I have some business over there with my people and then we'll go and do something on our own later. We came to Dragasevac. He got out of the car. I had no reason to get out of the car, had no business there. Why would I go out just to listen to the orders he was giving? He had his own job, his own assignment. He had his own purpose for being there. I had my own. That's all. Why would I go out to hear what Pecanac had to say to his men, to be some kind of advertising, promotion, whatever.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Could I have 65 ter 31461D, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: This is an intercept from 24 July you're familiar with, Mr. Popovic, about a man named Himzo Mujic who was exhumed from the Bisina mass grave. In other words, he was murdered at Bisina and buried there and later found. So this intercept is from the day after. And somebody is calling, X is saying: "He was at our place, I don't know if he still is, Himzo Mujic. "That's what I'm calling you for, man. "Yes. "Is it possible to find out where he is ..." I don't have time to go through every line of this, but if you look down a bit further, what's clear is that somebody is calling trying to get Himzo Mujic out of where he's being held. And X says, after saying about how he used to work for them: "So that's why he hopes he might be exchanged. But he told Neso almost everything about the area we're from and our people. What they had done and who did what to whom and that sort of thing." And then Y says: "And where is he? And X says: "I" --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Do we have correct page in B/C/S?

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: No, I think we need to go to the second page.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Then there's a discussion about calling the warden at the prison and a discussion saying: "Well, we can take care of it through Crna Rijeka, say that we really need that guy ... we need him down there in the field." Now, you know that Himzo Mujic was pulled out of the mass grave in Bisina; right? You know that as you sit here today, I mean, after your trial?

utterances.speaker: VUJADIN POPOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: And you know that the prisoners came from -- who were murdered in Bisina came from Susica prison; right? You know that as you sit here today?

utterances.speaker: VUJADIN POPOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Your Honours, may that be marked for identification, and I'll -- it's an intercept and we'll try to admit it later. It's not admitted at this stage.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Did we not hear about the notebook, authenticity of the notebook in general? Mr. Robinson, if --

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes, I don't know about this particular notebook, if this was included in -- but was this admitted in the Popovic case?

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: This was admitted in Popovic. It was admitted in Tolimir. My recollection is that we tried to admit it through a bar table, but we did not completely cite the transcript, I think, of the decision, which is why it was --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Very well --

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: -- not admitted previously. Unless there's no objection I would tender it now.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: No, let's be clear. Let's marked for identification and resolve it at a later stage.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: It receives MFI number -- Exhibit Number MFI P6499, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] May I? May I ask if there is an audio recording so we can identify it?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: We discuss the issue when we have the intercept operator or the commander.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Could I have P --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yeah, it can be sorted out outside the courtroom, if necessary at all. Let's continue.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Could I have P04776.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: This is an intercept from the same day, again you're familiar with it, Mr. Popovic, about one hour -- just a little over an hour later. It's the same frequency, same channel. And here X makes it clear that he is in Vlasenica, at the top where he says: "They're falling around us here," bombs. Y says: "No, really? Where? And X says: "Well, around Vlasenica."

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: If we go to page 2 of the English. I think we can stay on page 1 for now of the Serbian.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: We saw that in the intercept an hour earlier on the 24th of July somebody was calling and asking if they could basically save Himzo Mujic. And here X responds: "And another thing. Since I'm having difficulty reaching Kane up there," we saw Kane on the previous exhibit -- intercept, "tell him this Himzo Mujic. "Y: Mujic? "Himzo is no longer in prison here. He should call Lieutenant-Colonel Popovic" --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Do we not need the second page.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Now second page of the Serbian. I apologise.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: "Himzo is no longer in prison here" --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Could you check whether this is correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: This is correct, I believe. Yeah.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: "Himzo is no longer in prison there. He should call Lieutenant-Colonel Popovic. "Y: Lieutenant-Colonel? "X: Popovic. Ask for the switchboard of the Drina Corps and then for extension 91. "Drina Corps switchboard, extension 91. "X: Yes. And he should arrange it personally with him. He's the only one who knows where he went from here and what happened to him. You can do it if you see him somewhere during the day ..." So the person at Vlasenica who knows that Himzo Mujic is gone, calling back to tell Kane it's too late, there's only one person who can say where he went and what happened to him, and that's you because you were in charge of this murder operation, this small murder operation by July 1995 standards?

utterances.speaker: VUJADIN POPOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mr. Nicholls, first of all, I was not in charge of that murder operation, as I've told you before, and I think I was clear. Two, these X and Y who are calling suppose that I should know where this person is. Why would I know? If somebody wants a list of these people in prison, I can always get that list from the prison. I don't even remember that Susica was even exclusively our prison. I don't know when these people arrived there and whether I received a list or didn't receive that list. I don't know. I cannot comment on other people's conversations.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Your Honour, actually -- did you say 12.30 we'd break? I'd prefer now because I'm going to move on --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: [Overlapping speakers] --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: We'll have a break. We'll have a break for 45 minutes and resume at quarter past 1.00. --- Luncheon recess taken at 12.26 p.m.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Please continue, Mr. Nicholls.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. I may at the end of my time be asking for additional 15 to 20 minutes. I just wanted to let you know to -- because there's one additional topic that came up that I may try to cover. Just -- thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Okay. Still on Bisina, Mr. Popovic. You said you were not in charge of that murder operation. Let's keep talking about this murder -- incidents of murder, 23rd July, which, let's say, you're implementing for the command, not in charge of.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Could I have 65 ter 25593, please. This is an ICMP report on the Bisina grave-site from 2008. If we could go to English page 9, Serbian page 13, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: And before that comes up, I'll just read to you a part I'm not going to bring up. This is on page 4 of the English, just that it says that 39 bodies were recovered in this mass grave. Okay. 42. "Twenty-seven individuals were recovered with their hands behind their backs in direct association with ligatures made of grey-coated telephone wire on one or both wrists. Four victims had blindfolds. There was no evidence of proper burial." Now, where were their hands tied, Mr. Popovic? At the scene? Before they got put in the truck? Where did they bind these men?

utterances.speaker: VUJADIN POPOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: You're asking me something I don't know. I don't know where their hands were tied.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: All right.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Could I have 65 ter 03958 -- oh, excuse me. May I admit this report, Your Honour?

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBINSON
utterances.text: I object, Mr. President. No basis to do that through this witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: It's the witness's mass grave. He's going to -- he said he put these people in the ground, and I'm sure when I ask him --

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Mr. Popovic, when you got there, whenever you were there, let's not talk about when you got there, okay, you saw that these victims had their hands tied behind their backs, didn't you, before they were put in the grave?

utterances.speaker: VUJADIN POPOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I didn't see that. I really didn't. Really, I don't remember that at all. I didn't see it. Why? I would say if I did.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Mr. --

utterances.speaker: VUJADIN POPOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I just said: Bury them and --

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Okay. The witness has just commented that people were buried at Bisina. This is a report of the Bisina --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: But why did the Prosecution not have the time or opportunity to tender this earlier on?

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Well, we could have, Your Honour, but I didn't know that they were going to call the person who was present at the mass execution -- at this execution, which is why I'm using it now.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] This is a new situation for me, really.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: The Chamber does not think that we have a basis to admit this document through this witness. We'll not admit this at this time.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: 03958, please. Could we go to page 2, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: All right, Mr. Popovic, it's the exhumation photo from the Bisina mass grave. You said earlier about this mass grave: "It's the only grave where the bodies were properly laid in. You can see that from the record of exhumation." So these are how you properly laid the men into the grave; right?

utterances.speaker: VUJADIN POPOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Saying that, I had in mind -- I think that, first of all, you show the report of Amor Masovic - unless I'm mistaken - where that was written. And when I said: Bury them now, I turned away and left. I did not inspect what they would actually do and how. But it's an undisturbed grave and that's what it is. Now, how they did it, they used a machine and then dropped the bodies from it. I really -- I mean, when I said that, I had that report in mind because we had the report, as far as I remember. Maybe I'm mistaken but --

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Well, wait a minute. You just took credit, you just said in your defence, the way I read it and the way any plain reading would be, that this was the only grave where they were laid out properly and this is a grave where the men are lined up, not piled in a heap.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Sorry to interrupt, Mr. Nicholls. But, first of all, we need to establish this is the Bisina grave.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: I can make an offer of proof of that. This witness can't say -- I don't think he can say from this photograph.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: In e-court the title of this exhibit says: Photographs of exhumation at Budak, Kamenica 9, and other grave-sites, and that some photos tells Budak -- I'm not sure whether it is Bisina. Could you establish that first.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: The description may be wrong in e-court, but if necessary I could call our investigator. But we received these as a direct RFA for the Bisina grave-site. And this is the same grave that Himzo Mujic was brought out of. This came from the BH Federal Commission of Missing Persons.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Can you explain the date on this -- appearing on this photo?

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: No, Your Honour. It's just something with the camera. I don't know why the date --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: The first page shows 10th of July?

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Yes. I don't know why that date is there. But this is -- if we were to go back to the --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I doubt that that's it.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: If we were to go back to the prior exhibit, Your Honour, it describes the location and has some photographs. And it is the same location, the Bisina grave.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, I will leave it at that. Please continue.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Thank you. If we could go to --

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: Just, for the record, thank you, Excellency. I should have done it as well as posed questions about the textile. It doesn't look --

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Objection --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: That's an improper intervention during the cross-examination. You can take up the issue in your re-examination, Mr. Karadzic. Please continue, Mr. Nicholls.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Could we go to the next page, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: There we see one of the telephone wire ligatures described in the report, right, Mr. Popovic? You still don't remember that?

utterances.speaker: VUJADIN POPOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I said no, I don't remember because I didn't see that on the bodies there. I didn't go from one body to another to inspect them. When I came there, I just said nicely, as far as I remember -- there was this small area and bodies were scattered all around and it looked so awful that I felt lost there. I turned around and I said: Come on, bury them. First of all they didn't want to do it. And then I said: Please, do bury them. And then I turned around and left. Now, whether they -- I cannot assert, but I'm telling you that as opposed to the other graves that we were shown, this one is quite different. There everything was --

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Okay --

utterances.speaker: VUJADIN POPOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: -- intermingled, and here --

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Okay. And the burial machinery was there, right, right when you were there?

utterances.speaker: VUJADIN POPOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. The machine -- or rather, I don't remember how the excavator arrived. When I was passing by, I think it was by the barracks.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: My point is you were there when the bodies were loaded into the excavator and put in the grave?

utterances.speaker: VUJADIN POPOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, no, no. Just the first several bodies. At first they didn't want to do it, as I said, and then they loaded them into the excavator and began moving them further on.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: That's my point, the --

utterances.speaker: VUJADIN POPOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: But I didn't --

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: -- the excavator was there when you were there. You were there at the same time as the excavator which loaded the bodies; you just said that. Right?

utterances.speaker: VUJADIN POPOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I said I don't remember when it arrived. I remember that when I passed, it seems to me that it was parked next to the barracks. Whether it arrived after me or -- I don't remember.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: That's not the question. That's not the question.

utterances.speaker: VUJADIN POPOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Or before me.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: You answered the question. You were there when it picked up the bodies. You've answered that.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Could we go to the next page, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Okay. This is the orderly burial, it's a bit closer up. You think this is a -- you're saying this is one of the better burials?

utterances.speaker: VUJADIN POPOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, that is why I referred to the report which they made. As far as I remember, in the last sentence of the report it was said that the bodies were neatly placed. When I said and told them to bury them, they started working properly. And then I simply left because I couldn't stand being there any longer.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Okay --

utterances.speaker: VUJADIN POPOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: This doesn't look to me -- I have to say, to me this doesn't look like -- if that is really that, if that's the grave, it doesn't look like it, not to me.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: And -- so you didn't say: Line these people up in a row? That's just a -- you didn't direct the burials to be respectful by lining people in a row rather than piling them in a heap; right?

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Could we go to the last page, please.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Am I supposed to answer? I didn't literally tell them: Line them in rows. I told them: Bury them. And I believe that implied how that should be done and they knew how it should be done.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Page 8, please. Sorry, that's not the one I want.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Now, again I'll ask you -- you said the bodies were scattered around all over the place, right, when you got there. You didn't notice that their hands were tied behind their backs with wire ligatures, telephone wire, as we see here?

utterances.speaker: VUJADIN POPOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, Mr. Nicholls, because there were ferns and grass growing there quite high, 20 or 30 centimetres, and because of that you couldn't really see. It was in July, when there's so much vegetation growing. Perhaps I might have noticed, but I didn't really look that closely. I didn't focus on any single body. I was just looking at the whole scene.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Yeah, and the whole scene was that 27 out of these 39 bodies had their hands bound behind their backs?

utterances.speaker: VUJADIN POPOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's what the report says.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: So even if we were to accept your story, which, to make clear for the record, I don't for one minute, it's contradicted by the evidence of you being there during the executions, your response to arriving at a scene -- even if we believe you, your response to arriving at a scene on the 23rd of July when there are 39 victims, 27 of whom have their hands tied behind their backs, is just to bury them on the spot; right? You don't --

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBINSON
utterances.text: Excuse me, Mr. President. I think it's -- excuse me.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] To be buried on the spot, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. President, I don't believe it's proper for a lawyer to say that: I don't believe your story for one minute. What Mr. Nicholls believes or doesn't believe is completely irrelevant and it's improper for him to have said that. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: What I mean is, and perhaps I should have asked it differently, is in asking questions about his story, it does not mean accepting it and the position of the Prosecution is that that story is a lie, which is fair to put to the witness when I'm asking him questions about his story.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: I think the witness is entitled to answer the question. If you like, Mr. Popovic. Would you like to comment on that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] You mean the claim that the whole story is a lie? Only if there is no document that would support that. If there are documents which support what I'm telling, I don't see why that would be a lie. Perhaps it suits the Prosecutor or perhaps it doesn't, but I have come here and I have given the oath that I would be telling the truth rather than that I would be telling what Mr. Prosecutor wants to hear. There have been many such witnesses here who talked what they wanted -- what the OTP wanted to hear.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Your Honours, I would tender these photographs I've shown.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. President, I think it would be better if they were marked for identification, subject to showing the provenance of those photographs. Then if you're convinced of the provenance, they can be admitted in full.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: For example, Mr. Nicholls, can you see -- upload page 14 of the previous document, ICMP summary report --

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Excellency --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Just a second. Although we didn't admit it. Page 14, e-court page 14 of 65 ter number 25593.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: What I wanted to ask to be clarified, whether Mr. --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: I'll give you an opportunity. Like this. There you see the marking of Bisina.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: But in this set of photographs, i.e., 65 ter 3908 which you are tendering now, I don't see any of them. I see other markings for other places. So how are we satisfied -- we are satisfied that this photo depicts Bisina mass grave?

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Well, the photos that I've shown, Your Honours, separately from this report do not have the same markings, must have been taken at a different time before those markings were put down. We can see there were just red flags there, but there aren't the names of any other locations. And if you were to look, Your Honours --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: But then why does this set of photos have different marking like Budak or something -- if you go on, you can see Budak or something like that, it is a set of photos seems to be --

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Only page 1 to 8 of these documents -- of the photos are Bisina. I went too far when I went to page 9 before, to the last page, so there is an extra photo in there.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, I will hear your objection, Mr. Karadzic.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Can I make one more point, Your Honour, first?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: If you take a look at -- I'm sorry, I don't have the e-court page, but what is annex 3 to the Bisina report that we have in front of us -- page 13 in the English. All right. And if we were to look now, if we can do it on the split screen on page 5 of the photos that I was bringing up, 65 ter 03958, we go to page -- photo 5, you can see there that the outline is virtually identical and the machine in the back. It's a different -- it's not exactly the same photograph, but it's the same location. And you can see that even the excavator in the back -- and I'm not saying this is dispositive, but it does link these up and I can, if necessary, as I said, call an investigator. But this, I think, also shows that we're talking about the same spot.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Karadzic.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I'm going to ask the Colonel about these photographs during the re-examination. Could we please have photograph 8, or rather, page 8 --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: No, just tell us whether you have any objection to the admission and why.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I just wanted to ask whether Mr. Nicholls claims that it was tied on the back, photograph 8, hands tied on the back. Is that what he is saying? But I cannot ask the witness that. As I dispute this photograph, I am cautioning about this.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: And I can just say I won't be answering any questions from Mr. Karadzic about what these photographs show.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBINSON
utterances.text: Excuse me, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: The Chamber will mark it for -- these photos for identification until it is satisfied with its provenance.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: It receives MFI number P6500, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Now, you said just before the break how you were -- why didn't I relocate this? Why didn't I move this with all the other graves? And I'm going to put it to you why you didn't, because the mass graves at Kravica, Orahovac -- well, the execution sites at Kravica, Orahovac, Petkovci dam, Branjevo, all had survivors, all were notorious, and there were reports on these areas soon after and they were huge mass graves. So you didn't - I'm putting to you - move this relatively small mass grave because you felt it would not be discovered. It was 39 people, we don't know of any survivor of this grave -- of this execution, and it was in the mountains in Bisina which is why you didn't move it.

utterances.speaker: VUJADIN POPOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Oh, Mr. Nicholls, really, you can always take a person by surprise with your conclusions. I mean, after this execution people gathered there further away from that place, towards the hill, that's where the defence line was, I think, of the Sekovici Brigade. And people were passing by. It's close to the road.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Well --

utterances.speaker: VUJADIN POPOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: There were people right there who would come there.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Yes, local people and that's not who I'm talking about.

utterances.speaker: VUJADIN POPOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Why?

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: I'm not talking about local people. I'm talking about internationals finding out. And you also said this is the only primary mass grave. What about Cerska, another relatively small one by Drina Corps standards in July 1995, is that a primary or a secondary grave?

utterances.speaker: VUJADIN POPOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I heard of Cerska when I came here. I have no idea about Cerska. But I repeat, this grave was discovered through the local population as far as I know. So again, I repeat, once again what I said stands. Had I felt responsible, I would have relocated it. Why would that bother me? But you don't want to believe anything I'm saying. Well, you're entitled to that.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: And you don't -- when you stumble across, according to you, this mass grave, you don't take any steps to identify who these people are. You don't treat it like a crime scene. Even if your statement was to be given any credit, the first thing you do is try to cover the whole thing up; right? Bulldoze the bodies into the grave?

utterances.speaker: VUJADIN POPOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, what could I do at the crime scene where I felt lost, if you will? I simply said what I said, turned around, and left. Really, I was so shaken. I was lost.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Another thing you say in your statement, at paragraph 88, is that you were very upset when you came to this execution site and saw that all the prisoners were dead because you'd hoped that they could be exchanged for your cousin Djordje, right? That's in your statement paragraph 88.

utterances.speaker: VUJADIN POPOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: So that means that on the 23rd of July, 1995, the Drina Corps -- you can't find another prisoner for your cousin Djordje. You didn't save anybody from Kravica, Orahovac, Pilica, Branjevo, Petkovci, in order to exchange?

utterances.speaker: VUJADIN POPOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, really, that's not what it means. That is not what it means because the commission for exchanges that was conducted by Novakovic and my conversation with Tolimir, you see that I say to him, please -- about this exchange, that's what I meant. And now whether there were others, whether that was being sent, I wasn't thinking about that at that moment.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Yeah, but what it says in your statement which you or you wrote in consultation with people recently is that on that day you were upset because you thought: Oh, I could have exchanged these prisoners for my cousin. That's got nothing to do with what you were thinking at the time.

utterances.speaker: VUJADIN POPOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Well, yes. I thought what I wrote.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: And so would you agree with this statement: It's correct that these people we just saw in those photos were buried in a certain order and in a dignified manner? Do you think that's a dignified way to bury people?

utterances.speaker: VUJADIN POPOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mr. Nicholls, I see this grave. I'm confused by the dates on some of these photographs. At one moment it's the 18th of --

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Stop, stop --

utterances.speaker: VUJADIN POPOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: -- of October, and some other moment it is --

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Stop, stop. Forget the photos. Forget the photos. When you were there -- forget the photos. Take that out of my question. Do you think it's a dignified -- do you think the people who were buried in Bisina with heavy machinery were buried in a certain order and in a dignified manner? I'm just asking your opinion on that statement.

utterances.speaker: VUJADIN POPOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Up until now when I saw this photograph, that's what I thought and I told you why I said that, because I read that report where it says that the bodies were laid in order.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Paragraph 1156 of your trial judgement states that: "The Trial Chamber is satisfied that the ten wounded Bosnian Muslim men were killed sometime around 23 July. The Trial Chamber is further satisfied, based on the evidence above, that these men were placed in the custody of Popovic around 23 July." And then it goes on to say: "... the Trial Chamber finds that Popovic killed or facilitated the killing of the ten wounded Bosnian Muslim prisoners from Milici Hospital." Same day, 23rd July. My only question to you about that, the only question: Would you please tell us where those corpses were dumped because they haven't been found yet, other than one person?

utterances.speaker: VUJADIN POPOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Sincerely, Mr. Nicholls, if I knew I would have told you. Very frankly. I have no reason to hide that, but I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Your Honours, there was some discussion about the provenance. I'd like to have about 15 or so minutes more, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Please proceed. Continue.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. President, would it be okay if I have Mr. Krajisnik come back tomorrow, even though there may be a little bit of time left over?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: That's a safer option. We may take it.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBINSON
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Okay. Could I have P04592, please. Your Honours, this is a new document, it wasn't on my list, but I notified my friend that I would be using it.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Now just asking you, Mr. Popovic, you talked about the reburial operation and being in charge -- being involved, let me not say "in charge," being involved in the aspect of the use of the fuel. Very simply, there's been other evidence in this case I won't go into on the -- you spoke about that at page 61 today, on the reburial operation I don't want to go into. But very simply, this document concerns the fuel use for that reburial; right?

utterances.speaker: VUJADIN POPOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: And P04593 which is related to the document we just saw, same thing, right, related to the reburial, it's about the reburial?

utterances.speaker: VUJADIN POPOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Thank you. Okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Now, could I have P01473, please. This is a diary of General Mladic -- notebook of General Mladic, not diary. English page 310, please, Serbian 314. I'll go through this rather -- yeah, we were on the right page in the English. 310, please. 314 in the Serbian. And this is 22nd of August, 1995, 1.00 p.m., meeting with General Smith. Present, General Mladic has written down: Colonel Djurdjic, Indjic, Kusic, Krunic, Kosoric, Suka - if we go to the next page in English - Popovic, Furtula, I, and interpreter Tijana.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: I'm not going to ask you all about the content of this meeting, but do you remember being with General Mladic and these people in Borike and with Mr. Kosoric?

utterances.speaker: VUJADIN POPOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I do remember absolutely, and then General Mladic had his picture taken with General Smith. They exchanged caps and they were riding horses. And I'll explain why I was present there if you're interested.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Not at the moment, thanks.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: If we could go to page 315 in the English and page 319 in the Serbian.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: I don't want to go page by page, but this is General Smith speaking that Mladic is writing down. "They equate you with people, you are accused of being a war criminal, but that does not necessarily mean you are ..." Do you remember Smith saying that to General Mladic?

utterances.speaker: VUJADIN POPOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: This I do not remember exactly. It went through an interpreter. I really do not remember this. The meeting started in a very vociferous way. There were some heavy words that were heard, and then when things loosened up, then they were roasting a lamb on a spit and so on. But what they were discussing, I cannot remember the details.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Okay. Now I want to show you a video you've seen before from this time. We showed this same video to Mr. Kosoric when he was here in this trial. And you'll see yourself with Svetozar Kosoric, the Drina Corps intelligence chief, and Zoran Sarkic, Rogatica security.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Sorry, P06335.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: I don't know why there's no sound, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Do you hear any sound, Mr. Popovic?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Do you remember having watched this video?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I remember the video footage very well. I watched it during our trial, and I know even what can be heard in the background. I can explain that --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Then why don't you put your question.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: If we could just play the video to the spot I want to stop. Your Honours, I'm sorry, it's without the sound and there are some spots where Mr. --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Because Mr. Popovic said he remembered the footage as well as the sound.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Yeah.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: I think you can safely put the question.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: All right. Let's continue.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: I don't see a point of continuing. Just put your question, Mr. Nicholls.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Let's go to 2.53.2. Go back a bit. Go back a bit. Play it.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Pause.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: That's Svetozar Kosoric next to you, right, you've got your arm around him. That's you next to him. You're on the right as we look at the screen?

utterances.speaker: VUJADIN POPOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's right.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: We're at 2.43.3.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: This is that same time as that meeting with General Mladic; right? 22nd August?

utterances.speaker: VUJADIN POPOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Here, in this place? No. This is Rogatica --

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Rogatica --

utterances.speaker: VUJADIN POPOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, Rogatica, and it was some celebration. There was some villa there. We had had a few drinks and -- did you see that reference to Mirabeau a moment ago?

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Yeah --

utterances.speaker: VUJADIN POPOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I was reciting a poem by Jacques Prevert and ... yeah.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Rogatica, exactly, that's what Svetozar Kosoric said as well.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Keep playing.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Stop. I'll read it out to you: "Come on, the two moustachioed fellows, you know like this. Zoka, come over here, the entire OB is present. The war criminals."

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: We'll play it for one more second and then I'll ask you a question.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: All right. My question to you, Mr. Popovic, you told the truth there in this video, didn't you? That's a truthful statement coming right out of your mouth: You are a war criminal, a war criminal who jokes about it?

utterances.speaker: VUJADIN POPOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Oh, Mr. Nicholls, I said a moment ago we were at that celebration, we got drunk, we had had a few drinks, and we went outside and I said that, no doubt about that, but you have to understand in which context I said it. Because just on its own it doesn't mean a thing. At the very beginning of the war we had been declared war criminals, Radovan's Chetniks, Radovan's hillbillies. They called us all sorts of names, and this was the allusion that I was making. Come on here, all of us are war criminals. It's certainly not what you said. Also next to me is Svetozar Kosoric and Zoka Carkic. Neither one of them is accused. You see that this is just a joke, a benign joke, a drunken joke, if you will. You see how I'm behaving.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Yeah, but the funny thing about it is you make this joke and now you're sitting here convicted of genocide. So it's true, isn't it, what you said here? You are a war criminal?

utterances.speaker: VUJADIN POPOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Oh, really, I mean if I explain this sincerely, frankly, from the bottom of my heart and soul and you translate it into something different, then I'm speechless. I stand by what I said a moment ago. And now me being here ...

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Nicholls.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Mr. Karadzic, do you have any re-examination?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, I would like us just to call up that photograph number 8, to establish whether it matches the description. Otherwise, I have no other questions for Colonel Popovic. If you think it is unnecessary, then I'm not even going to ask about that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: No, it's up to you.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, P600, could that please be called up, photograph number 8.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] That's the photograph.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Colonel, sir, does it look like these hands had been tied in the back?

utterances.speaker: VUJADIN POPOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The picture is self-explanatory. It seems to me that it is in the front.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Thank you, Colonel, sir. I have no further questions for you.

utterances.speaker: VUJADIN POPOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: You're welcome.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: That concludes your evidence, Mr. Popovic. Thank you for your testimony. You may be excused. Thank you, Mr. Zivanovic, for your assistance as well.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, I would like to address you with a few words, if you allow me to do so?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: What is it about?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, about some things that the Prosecutor had not raised here. For instance, there is this very interesting intercept that was interpreted in a completely different way in our case and there is not a single person here that can clarify that better, and in my view it was represented in a completely different way there --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: I don't think it will assist the Chamber. We will not hear you this time.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. Thank you. I meant -- I mean, there is no one who can deal with it better than I can because I was the one who was speaking.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you for your testimony.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: Would the Chamber be interested in seeing what "balija" means?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: It's up to you, Mr. Karadzic.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: I tender it by bar table --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: No, no, no, you will have another opportunity to tender -- to elicit such evidence through a proper -- appropriate witness. Mr. Robinson, Judge Baird has a question for you.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBINSON
utterances.text: Very well. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BAIRD
utterances.text: Mr. Robinson, should the motion be granted and --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: It's about Krajisnik.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BAIRD
utterances.text: Yes. And the Prosecution is precluded from questioning the witness on statements he made in parliament, what would be the evidential value of those statements in the absence of cross-examination? I mean, how would you invite the Chamber to approach that evidence?

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBINSON
utterances.text: I think it would be approached in the same way as you would approach evidence from other witnesses whose statements are introduced in transcripts of Assembly sessions but who have not appeared here. So basically you -- I wouldn't be asking you to disregard that evidence simply because the witness had asserted a privilege as to explaining it. So I think you would give it the same weight as if he hadn't appeared.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BAIRD
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MORRISON
utterances.text: But isn't there a qualitative difference between a witness who is -- does not attend and is not required to attend and one who is specifically called?

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBINSON
utterances.text: Well, there is, but in terms of taking the text of -- let's just take an example of something Mr. Krajisnik said -- well, on the 18th of March, 1992, in an Assembly session, in which his Trial Chamber has found that this was a call to arms. So if he doesn't come and explain -- isn't questioned about that, you are free to interpret from the transcript of the Assembly session in whatever way you believe the other evidence, including other things he may say about the war and the events in general, lead you to conclude. So I don't think that it's -- the fact that he has appeared as a witness here makes your job any different. If that isn't addressed, then you take what evidence you do have in the record and assess it based upon all the other evidence that you have.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Mr. Robinson, this is from your summary of Mr. Krajisnik's evidence to be tendered. I quote: "Mr. Krajisnik will describe the significant issues that arose in the Assembly during 1991 and 1992 ..." And further: "He will also testify about the speeches by -- made by Dr. Karadzic to the common Assembly as well as the interventions of others during the Assembly sessions ..." And it goes on: "He will explain that there was never any plan or policy for a pure Serbian entity or to explore -- or expel Muslims or Croats from areas controlled by the Bosnian Serbs." So one can consider that he's being called due to his role as speaker of the Republika Srpska Assembly, and therefore the statements made at these sessions are such an intrinsic part of his testimony that it would not be fair to the Prosecution to proceed without cross-examination on these issues. What would you say to that -- such observation?

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. President, the -- as you can see from that summary, it makes no reference to his own interventions at the Assembly session. So he -- his testimony will include statements that are made at the Assembly sessions at which he presided but not his own interventions, because we think the privilege is limited to his own interventions. And so I believe he is -- can testify and can be compelled to testify about what was said at the Assembly by others but not by him.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: So he cannot be questioned as to the authenticity of the transcript?

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBINSON
utterances.text: I think he can be questioned about the authenticity of the transcript other than as to his own statements.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MORRISON
utterances.text: How could privilege or immunity extend to authenticity? I can see what you might say, that if he testifies that they're authentic then claims privilege. But surely the -- privilege only arises if the Court is satisfied that the transcripts are, in fact, authentic.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBINSON
utterances.text: Well, I think he -- if he's being asked: Did you say something -- here's the recording of what you are reported to have said at the Assembly, is that what you said? I think he has a privilege to -- not to answer that question. On the other hand, if he's asked: Is this -- are these statements made by Assemblymen such and such consistent with your recollection or does the transcript in general, does that appear to be faithful to the discussion as you recall it? Other than dealing with his own statements, I think he could answer those questions. But if he says: Yes, this transcript is -- or if he's required to say: Yes, this transcript is what I said, then we're -- we have essentially questioned him about what he has said in parliament, which is what we say is privileged.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MORRISON
utterances.text: So you wouldn't draw a distinction between what is said and what is the consequence or object or understanding to be drawn from the words used?

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBINSON
utterances.text: Well, I would say that he can't be questioned about anything about what he said. That's the best I can say from the language of the Bill of Rights and the United States Constitution.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: I take it the witness has been released?

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Okay. Then unless there's anything to be raised, the hearing is adjourned. Yes, Mr. Tieger.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: I gathered that the Court didn't want further argument, it's just to add some specific inquiries from Mr. Robinson which it is deliberating about --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Well, if you wish to, you can add something.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: All right. Well, I may raise them again further, but Mr. Robinson has again reverted to arguing that anything he cites from the US Constitution has entered customary international law. That's all he could cite before. Then he attempted to distinguish from the rest of his authorities which involved the conflation of immunity and privilege that he argued against before. Whatever domestic jurisprudence provides, and again, we haven't been provided with an adequate answer of even what the circumstances are in domestic jurisdictions when they apply and whether they would apply in any domestic jurisdiction to a situation like this, we certainly don't have an answer for its applicability in international jurisprudence. We continue to assert that this is a misuse of the invocation of certain limited standards from domestic jurisdictions. But in any event, I simply wanted to note the question the Court originally raised, and that was the fairness of using affirmatively in some way the propositions that rely upon the alleged privilege that's being invoked and then running from it when it comes time for cross-examination. So what Mr. Robinson posits is the possibility that you could raise a discussion in which the accused participates, misleadingly characterise it, and then when it comes time to expose the misleading nature of that explanation by pointing to the accused or the witness's participation in that discussion, suddenly curtail the discussion, so that it can't be commented on. That seems to me, as the Court was suggesting in its question, cannot possibly be an approach that is countenanced by international law or any domestic jurisdiction either.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: If the Chamber comes to a conclusion that the statements he made at these Assembly sessions are such an intrinsic part, there's a possibility for the Chamber to conclude that his testimony should not be allowed at all. What would you say to that?

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBINSON
utterances.text: Well, we would have to discuss that among ourselves, but that may be something we would ask you for leave to appeal.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Very well. We'll continue tomorrow morning at 9.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: to be reconvened on Thursday, the 7th day of November, 2013, at 9.00 a.m. 20 21 22 23 24 25

procedural_notes.text: --- Whereupon the hearing adjourned at 2.25 p.m.,
